E01.title: Panting & pounding — causes, effects & constructional details
E01.answer_markdown:
a) Panting and pounding are two distinct types of local, dynamic stresses acting on the ship's structure forward
of the first collision bulkhead, primarily caused by the vessel's interaction with waves and its motion in rough
seas. They are separate mechanisms — one a cyclic pressure loading, the other an impact loading — and
because they are resisted by different structure they should be treated separately and not merged.
1. Panting: Panting is the in-and-out flexing of the shell plating, particularly at the fore end. Causes: It is
caused by rapidly alternating water pressures on the hull as waves pass along the ship's sides and the vessel
pitches (the vertical motion of the bow and stern). The loading is therefore a cyclic pressure variation arising
as the ends alternately immerse and emerge while the vessel pitches, not a single blow. Affected Areas: Fore
End — the primary area, specifically from the bow to the first collision bulkhead (roughly the forward 15% of the
ship's length, that is approximately the forward 0.15 L in the forepeak); After End — to a lesser degree, in the
aft peak area. Effects: Fatigue & Leaking (continuous flexing can lead to fatigue cracking in plating and
welding); Structural Damage (separation of the hull plating from internal stiffeners and decks); Weakened
Structure (severe structural deformation to side shell plating).
2. Pounding (Slamming): Pounding occurs when the ship's bow lifts out of the water in a heavy sea and then
crashes down upon the water surface. Causes: High-speed motion in rough head seas, particularly when the
ship is in a light or ballast condition. Affected Areas: Fore Bottom (the flat bottom plating in the forward of the
ship, over approximately the forward 25–30% of the length); Fore Shoulder (the forward side shell). Pounding
is thus a sudden impact load on the flat of bottom forward after it has emerged in a light or ballast trim, and
not a pressure cycle. Effects: Severe Damage (dents, buckling, and rupture of the bottom plating); Structural
Failure (deformed internals, floors and girders); Whipping Stresses (the sudden impact causes the entire hull
girder to vibrate, creating whipping stresses, which can lead to increased stress throughout the ship and
accelerated fatigue).
b) To resist panting and pounding stresses in the forepeak region where these forces are most affected,
following constructional details are implemented. Each detail belongs to one of the two forces: panting is
resisted by the stringers, beams and breast hooks that stiffen the shell transversely, while pounding is resisted
by the heavy bottom grillage and thickened plating.
1. Panting Stringers: Triangular horizontal girders fitted on the side frames, spaced about 2m apart vertically,
connecting the side frames to the collision bulkhead.
2. Panting Beams: Metal beams fitted horizontally at alternate frames, connecting the port and starboard
panting stringers to stiffen the structure transversally to counteract the in-and-out flexing of the shell plating
caused by panting. Where beams are not fitted, a perforated wash flat or deep beams may be used in the peaks
to perform the same function.
3. Breast Hooks: Horizontal triangular plates connecting port and starboard panting stringers at the centre
line at the bow, providing extra rigidity to the stem plating.

4. Increased Plating Thickness: Strengthened Shell Plating especially the bottom shell plating is significantly
thickened in the forward 25% of the ship's length (pounding zone) to withstand high-impact loads.
5. Solid Plate Floors and Wash Bulkhead: Solid plate floors, fitted at every frame in the pounding region
and supported by strengthened pillars/ wash bulkhead, together with intercostal side girders spaced not
more than about 2.2 m apart, and reduced transverse frame spacing (reduced to not more than 700 mm),
provide a robust foundation that helps absorb and distribute the forces generated. The wash bulkhead in the
fore peak additionally limits free-surface movement when the peak is ballasted.

E03.title: Six degrees of motion & the structure that resists them
E03.answer_markdown:
(a) Six Degrees of Motion a Ship Experiences in Heavy Weather
The six motions divide into three translational motions — surge (longitudinal), sway (transverse) and heave
(vertical) — and three rotational motions — roll (about the longitudinal axis), pitch (about the transverse axis)
and yaw (about the vertical axis).
• Surge: Forward and backward motion along the length of the ship, typically due to waves or propulsion
forces.
• Heave: Vertical motion of the ship as it rises and falls with the waves.
• Sway: Lateral motion from side to side, caused by wind or wave action.
• Roll: Tilting motion from side to side around the longitudinal axis, often caused by wave action.
• Pitch: Rotational motion about the transverse axis, where the bow and stern move alternately.
• Yaw: Rotational movement around the vertical axis, changing the ship's heading due to wind or waves.
A further distinction is worth stating because it governs part (b): only heave, roll and pitch have a
hydrostatic restoring force, so that the ship is naturally pushed back towards equilibrium and the motion is
oscillatory. Surge, sway and yaw have no restoring force and are therefore controlled by propulsion, the
rudder and steering gear, and by mooring, rather than being resisted by structure.
Original sketch — the six degrees of motion (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.47
b) Constructional details that are designed to resist forces exerted on a ship by the SIX degrees of motion are;
• Rolling: Bilge keels/stabilizers/anti roll tanks are specifically engineered to handle, dissipate, or resist rolling
forces.
• Yawing: Highly effective, high-aspect ratio rudder and its associated robust steering gear absorb yawing
forces. Strictly, the rudder and steering gear are control devices rather than resisting structure, since yaw
has no hydrostatic restoring force.

• Pitching, and Surging: High tensile steel strengthened bottom structure with stiffeners, bulbous bow,
panting stringers and panting beams forward and aft absorbs the pitching and surging forces. Pitch and
heave, and the slamming they cause, are resisted principally by the strengthened bottom forward and
deep floors, assisted by the bulbous bow.
• Heaving and Swaying: High tensile steel strengthened double Hull, double Bottom structures absorb
heaving forces. Sheer strake, bilge strake, garboard strake and keel strake designs contribute to longitudinal
strength absorbing swaying forces. Sway, like surge and yaw, is controlled rather than structurally
resisted; the continuous longitudinal material named here provides the hull-girder strength that carries the
resulting loads.
Source note: Part 1's answer describes structure as “absorbing” sway and yaw forces. Its own Model Additions correct this —
those two motions, with surge, have no hydrostatic restoring force and are controlled by the rudder, propulsion and mooring.
Both readings are shown above so the distinction the examiner is testing is not lost.

E04.title: Hull stresses in heavy weather & the structure that resists them
E04.answer_markdown:
a) Stresses the hull of an ocean-going vessel is subjected to when it encounters heavy weather are;
The governing design case is the longitudinal bending of the hull girder, which is the sum of the still-
water bending moment and the wave bending moment — hogging when a crest is amidships and sagging
when the ship sits in a trough. Acting with it are shear forces, greatest near the quarter-length points, and, in
oblique seas, torsion, which is important for open-deck ships. The section modulus of the deck and bottom
is sized to this combined bending moment, which is precisely why the continuous longitudinal material
listed in part (b) is provided.
i) Longitudinal Stresses — Hogging: when a ship is lifted at the mid ships by a wave crest, the center of the
vessel experiences upward bending, leading to tensile stresses at the deck and compressive stresses at the
bottom. Sagging: when the ends are lifted by waves and the midship section sinks, it creates downward
bending, resulting in compressive stresses at the deck and tensile stresses at the bottom.
ii) Transverse Stresses — Racking: rolling in heavy seas induces transverse stresses that can distort the
ship's structure, particularly affecting corners and joints. This stress is most significant at beam knees and tank
side brackets where the rectangular cross section of the ship tries to distort into a parallelogram sideways.
iii) Local Stresses — Panting: fluctuations in water pressure during wave action cause an in-and-out motion
of the hull plating, particularly at the fore end. Pounding: when a ship pitches heavily, it can slam down onto
waves, causing severe impacts on the forward structure. This results in high local stresses that necessitate
reinforced bottom structures.
iv) Water Pressure Effect: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth (as the ship heaves) and acts
perpendicularly on the ship's hull, especially below the waterline. This results in high local stresses that
necessitate hull design optimization, structural strengthening, and advanced material selection.
b) Construction details which resist the stresses acting on ships are;
1. Hogging and Sagging stresses are resisted by strengthening the uppermost deck and bottom shell plating
with continuous longitudinal members, so as to provide the section modulus required by the combined still-
water and wave bending moment. Key structural reinforcements include thickened sheer/bilge/garboard/keel
strakes, deck stringers, high-tensile steel, longitudinal bulkheads, and deep double-bottom girders.
2. Racking stresses are resisted by transverse bulkheads reinforced with large brackets, Extra-deep, strong
transverse frames (web frames), Beam Knees, Deck/Bilge Brackets, rounded sheer strake, and double bottom
box girder structure especially torsion boxes. The torsion boxes also carry the torsional loading imposed in
oblique seas.
3. Panting and Pounding stresses are resisted by panting stringers, panting beam, reduced frame spacing
(900 mm to 700 mm), deep plate floors, longitudinal/horizontal intercostal stringers supported by strengthened
pillars/wash bulkhead, and Strengthened Shell Plating especially significantly thickened bottom shell plating
with intercostal girders (spaced no more than 2.2 m apart).
4. Water pressure stresses are further resisted by V shaped hull, reduced fwd flared design, specialized x-
stern design and ship building using robust welding techniques with a combination of longitudinal and
transverse framing in addition to above design features.

Additions direct. Spell it correctly in the exam — it is a word markers notice.

E05.title: Five terms for hull distortion in heavy seas
E05.answer_markdown:
1. Hogging — Type of Stress: Longitudinal bending stress. Location: Occurs in the midship section of the
hull. When a ship is lifted at the mid ships by a wave crest, the center of the vessel experiences upward
bending, leading to tensile stresses at the deck and compressive stresses at the bottom.
2. Sagging — Type of Stress: Longitudinal bending stress. Location: Occurs in the midship area. When the
ends are lifted by waves and the midship section sinks, it creates downward bending, resulting in compressive
stresses at the deck and tensile stresses at the bottom.
3. Racking — Type of Stress: Transverse shear stress. Location: Racking is a dynamic transverse
deformation, due to transverse stresses, such as rolling or uneven wave action, where the rectangular cross-
section of the ship tries to distort into a parallelogram sideways. It can lead to distortion of the transverse
sections. The stress concentrates at the corners of the section — the beam knees, the tank-side
brackets and the frame-to-beam connections — and is worst when the ship is rolling in a light or ballast
condition.
4. Panting — Type of Stress: Localized dynamic stress. Location: Panting is the in-and-out flexing movement
of the ship's shell plating due to changes in water pressure near the bow and stern as the ship pitches in heavy
seas, affecting the forepeak most and the after peak to a lesser degree.
5. Whipping — Type of Stress: Longitudinal bending stress. Location: Occurs along the entire length of the
hull and is a transient, high-frequency vibration of the hull girder caused by severe slamming impacts in heavy
seas. The hull vibrates at its natural frequency, resulting in high-stress concentrations. More precisely it is a
transient longitudinal vibratory bending of the hull girder in its two-node mode, which decays after a
slam or bow-flare impact. The related condition springing — a steady, wave-excited hull vibration — is
accepted by some examiners as an alternative term.
Each of the five terms carries two marks, one for the stress type and one for the location, so both must be
named. If preferred, pounding / slamming or pitching may be substituted for any one of the five above; all
are valid conditions of hull distortion.

E06.title: Distortion effects & the structure that resists them
E06.answer_markdown:
a) Racking: Racking is a dynamic transverse deformation, due to transverse stresses, such as rolling or uneven
wave action, where the rectangular cross-section of the ship tries to distort into a parallelogram sideways. It can
lead to distortion of the transverse sections. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the
effect are; Transverse bulkheads · Side frames · Beam knees and pillars · Tank-side brackets · Web frames ·
Deck transverses — the corners of the section being where racking bites hardest.
b) Panting: Panting is the in-and-out flexing movement of the ship's shell plating due to changes in water
pressure near the bow and stern as the ship pitches in heavy seas. Component parts of the ship's structure,
which help resist the effect are; Panting beams and stringers · Breast hooks and panting frames in the forepeak
and aft peak · Deep or panting floors in the peaks · Reduced frame spacing forward.
c) Pounding: Pounding is the repetitive slamming of the ship's bow onto the water surface, especially in rough
seas, leading to localized stress. It acts over the flat of bottom in the forward approximately 25–30% of
the ship's length. Component parts of the ship's structure, which help resist the effect are; Reinforced bottom
structure in the fore part (e.g., floors, intercostals) · Strong framing and thicker bottom shell plating in the bow
area · Solid plate floors at every frame · Intercostal side girders not more than about 2.2 m apart ·
Increased bottom-shell thickness · Reduced frame spacing, not more than 700 mm.
d) Water Pressure Effect: Hydrostatic pressure increases with depth (as the ship heaves) and acts
perpendicularly on the ship's hull, especially below the waterline. Component parts of the ship's structure, which
help resist the effect are; Hull plating and stiffeners (longitudinal and frames) · Transverse bulkheads and
internal framing.
e) Dry docking Stresses: Stresses imposed on the hull when a ship is supported by keel blocks and bilge
blocks during dry docking. They peak at the keel during the critical period, when the stern has landed on the
blocks but the ship is not yet fully supported along its length. Component parts of the ship's structure, which
help resist the effect are; Keel structure (center girder, floors) · Strong transverse framing and double bottom
structure · Side girders, the whole double bottom acting as a stiff grillage to spread the block reactions.

E07.title: Bulkheads, wing tanks & double-bottom purposes
E07.answer_markdown:
a) Tanker vessels are divided by longitudinal bulkheads to improve structural strength, reduce free surface
effects (transverse movement of liquid), and enable the transport of multiple cargo grades. These bulkheads
strengthen the hull against bending and racking, prevent excessive listing, facilitate better control of cargo
weight distribution and damage stability.
b) Ore carriers are fitted with wing tanks primarily to improve stability by managing the high center of gravity
associated with dense iron ore cargoes (stiff ship) and to increase structural flexibility. These tanks allow for
better stability control, provide space for ballast, and can serve as protective double-hull structures, reducing
risks from grounding or collision.
The seakeeping reason is the headline mark. Dense ore stows low in the hold and leaves the ship excessively
stiff, that is with an unnecessarily large GM and therefore a very short, violent roll period. Carrying ballast in the
upper wing or topside tanks raises KG, which lengthens the roll period and eases the transverse
accelerations on the structure, the cargo and the crew. Alongside this, the sloping wing-tank plating gives the
hold a self-trimming hopper geometry, and the tanks form a double-skin space protecting the cargo hold
in a side collision or grounding.
c) Double bottom tanks in dry cargo ships serve critical structural and safety functions beyond carrying liquids.
They provide longitudinal strength, protect the hull during grounding, improve ship stability, and offer a robust
foundation for cargo/machinery while enabling emergency damage control by preventing flooding of cargo
holds.

d) Transverse watertight bulkheads are crucial in ship construction for maintaining structural integrity and
safety. They provide essential transverse strength, subdivide the hull to prevent progressive flooding, act as fire-
resistant barriers to localize blazes, and support decks.
• Subdivision for Flood Control: They divide the ship into watertight compartments, restricting flooding to
one area in the event of hull damage, thus preventing the entire vessel from sinking.
• Structural Strength and Rigidity: These bulkheads act as rigid, vertical sub divisions that enhance the
overall transverse strength of the hull, resist racking stresses, and maintain the ship's transverse form.
• Fire Subdivision: They act as fire-resistant partitions that limit the spread of fire from one compartment to
another, enabling the crew to isolate and extinguish fires in a specific zone.
• Structural Support for Decks: They provide vertical support for the deck structure above, enhancing the
ship's overall strength.
Two supporting points complete the answer. The collision bulkhead and the after-peak bulkhead are
themselves transverse watertight bulkheads required by SOLAS, which is the clearest illustration of the
flood-control function. The number of bulkheads required is set by the floodable-length and
subdivision calculation for the ship, not chosen arbitrarily.

E08.title: Container-ship strength with large hold openings
E08.answer_markdown:
Original sketch — container ship mid-ship half section (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.37
The governing problem in this ship type is torsion. Removing the deck to give the large hatch openings needed
for cargo access leaves an open cross-section with very low torsional stiffness, so that oblique or
quartering seas would twist and warp the hull. The purpose of the structure described below is to re-close
that section and restore the torsional strength lost with the deck.
Container ships maintain structural integrity, despite very large deck openings for cargo access, by utilizing
high-tensile steel, a double-hull construction for torsional rigidity, and large “box-shaped wing tanks” (torsion
boxes) that provide longitudinal strength. The U-shaped structure, reinforced with heavy transverse frames and
a deep double bottom, compensates for the lack of deck plating. Key Structural Elements are;
• Torsion Box (Wing Tanks): The most critical element, these large box girders run longitudinally along the
top edge of the side shells, providing immense torsional rigidity against twisting forces. Being closed box
sections, they carry the shear flow that the missing deck can no longer carry.
• Double Hull and Double Bottom: Essential for structural strength and damage stability, providing a rigid
base (double bottom) and side structure (double hull). The keel, bottom shell, tank top plating, the side shell
at the top, deck stringer plates and deck longitudinal help resist longitudinal stresses.

• Longitudinal Framing: The entire structure is longitudinally framed to handle large bending moments
(hogging/sagging).
• Transverse Bulkheads: Deep webs and strong transverse bulkheads are placed between cargo holds to
maintain transverse strength.
• Minimized Bilge Strake: The transition from bottom to side is angled or rounded with a minimal radius to
maximize cargo stowage, often eliminating traditional bilge strakes.
The construction method adopted in construction of a container ship is the “Box Girder” method. The design
uses Finite Element Method (FEM) to analyze and ensure the box girders can withstand the expected torsional
stresses. The box girder structure helps strengthen the side structure along the hatch side together with
continuous hatch coming and bulwark.
At hatch end covers, transvers box section connects the box girder together forming a very rigid structure. It is
this combination — closed box girders at the upper sides joined by transverse box sections at the
hatch ends — that re-closes the section and restores torsional strength. The combination of longitudinal
framing and double bottom construction provides enhanced stability and safety, ensuring that even with large
cargo access hatches, the ship remains seaworthy.
One further detail earns credit: the hatch corners are a known fatigue hot-spot because of the stress
concentration at the discontinuity, so they are radiused and insert-plated with higher-grade material and
checked by finite element analysis.

E09.title: Ship-construction terms (purpose & location)
E09.answer_markdown:
a) Duct keel is a longitudinal, watertight tunnel built into bulk carriers and container ship's double-bottom
structure, running along the centre line from the collision bulkhead to the forward engine room bulkhead. It
strengthens the ship's bottom structure, surviving longitudinal stresses. It houses vital pipes for ballast, fuel,
and bilge systems, allowing for easy inspection and maintenance. Its clear width is limited — commonly not
more than about 2 m — so that the double bottom either side of it remains structurally effective, and it is not
carried under the machinery space, where a solid centre girder is fitted instead. Being an enclosed space,
entry requires the full enclosed-space-entry procedure.
b) Bilge keels are narrow fins or plates attached amidships, longitudinally along the turn of the bilge, where
the bottom curves into the sides, on both sides. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance when the
vessel rolls, creating a damping effect that reduces the amplitude of rolling motions.
c) Collision bulkhead is the foremost, heavily reinforced, transverse watertight bulkhead in a ship, extending
from the bottom to the freeboard deck. Its purpose is to maintain vessel safety and buoyancy by restricting
flooding from the forepeak in a head-on collision, preventing water ingress to cargo holds. Its position is set by
SOLAS II-1 and the ICLL: not less than 0.05 L (or 10 m, whichever is the less) and not more than 0.08 L (or
0.05 L + 3 m) from the forward perpendicular at the load line. No openings or doors are permitted in it
below the freeboard deck, and only one pipe penetration is allowed, fitted with a screw-down valve
operable from above the freeboard deck.
d) Camber is the slight, parabolic, curvature (1/50 of the vessel's breadth) of a ship's exposed weather decks in
the transverse (athwartship) direction, where the deck is higher at the centre line than at the sides. The
classical value is therefore B/50 at midships, though modern ships often use a straight-line camber instead
of a parabola. Its purpose is to allow rain or seawater from waves to drain efficiently off the weather decks and
prevent accumulation. The upward curvature increases the deck's structural strength against bending, flexural
loads, and longitudinal deflection, and it also offsets the visual impression that the ship is hogged.
e) Flare refers to the outward curvature of the hull's side shell plating as it rises from the waterline toward the
main deck. It is essentially the widening of the hull section from bottom to top above the waterline. The highest
degree of flare is located at the forward end of the ship (the bow). The outward curvature acts as a deflector,
forcing water away from the deck. A flared hull increases reserve buoyancy, deck area and stability. The trade-
off is that excessive flare aggravates bow-flare slamming loads in head seas. The opposite form, where
the side shell curves inward as it rises, is called tumblehome.
Each part carries two marks and asks two things — purpose and location — so both must be given; a purpose
without a location loses half the mark.
Source note: Part 1 gives the collision-bulkhead position as “between 5% and 8% of the ship's length (L) or 10 m maximum
from forward”. Its own Model Additions record that this conflates two separate limits, and the corrected wording is used above.

E10.title: Bilge keels — damage prevention, testing, length
E10.answer_markdown:
a) i) Bilge keels are designed with a flexible structure, usually a bulb plate, welded to a flat bar doubler —
properly called a ground bar, an intercostal flat bar — which is then attached to the shell plating via double
continuous fillet welds. This design ensures that if the keel strikes an object, it tears away at the weld to the
doubler without damaging or breaching the main shell plating. The essential logic is a deliberate weak link:
the ground bar is continuously double-fillet welded to the shell directly over an internal longitudinal
or frame, while the keel-to-ground-bar weld is made the weaker joint, so that on impact the keel shears
off at that weld and the shell plating stays intact. The ground bar must always land on supported structure,
so that loads are never fed into unsupported shell plating. Key design and attachment features to prevent shell
damage are:
• Doubler Plate: The bilge keel is not welded directly to the shell; instead, a flat bar “doubler” is welded to
the shell plating, and the keel is welded to this doubler. This provides a sacrificial buffer zone.
• Weakened Connection (Soft Nose): The weld connecting the vertical plate of the keel to the flat bar
doubler is often designed to be weaker than the shell plating, acting as a breaking point.
• Internal Stiffening Alignment: The bilge keels are positioned directly in line with internal stiffeners (such
as transverse frames or longitudinal) to spread loading, rather than on unsupported, flexible shell plating.
• Rounded Ends (Scallops): The ends of the bilge keels are tapered or rounded to prevent stress
concentrations at the tip. The end is additionally snipped or soft-toed and aligned with internal structure,
so that the termination does not create a hard spot at which fatigue cracks would initiate.
• Limiting Length: They are typically restricted to 30%-60% of the ship's length amidships, avoiding areas
with high bending/twisting stresses, which reduces the chance of propagating cracks into the main hull.
(ii) Testing

The first point to make is that a solid bilge keel cannot be leak- or pressure-tested, since it encloses no
volume. Its integrity is judged instead by:
• Visual Inspection: During dry docking, the entire bilge keel is inspected for any damage, cracks, or
deformation.
• NDT (Non-Destructive Testing): Techniques such as ultrasonic testing or magnetic particle inspection may
be employed to assess the integrity of welds and detect any defects — in practice crack testing by MPI or
dye-penetrant of the welds.
• Hammer or percussion testing along the keel, to find sections that have detached from the ground bar.
• Examination of the weld toes for fatigue cracking, particularly at the ends and at any repair, carried
out at dry-dock.
b) Bilge keels are designed to extend only 30% to 60% of the vessel's length, primarily in the midship region.
Reasons for not extending Bilge keels to the full length include:
1. Increased Resistance and Drag: Extending the bilge keels along the full length would cause excessive
frictional drag, significantly increasing fuel consumption and reducing the vessel's speed.
2. Structural Damage Risk: The bow and stern areas are more prone to damage. If extended to the full
length, the bilge keels are at higher risk of being torn off due to slamming, maneuvering, or docking.
3. Optimal Effectiveness in Midship Region: The maximum roll damping occurs in the midship section,
where the bilge keels have the highest velocity relative to the hull's rolling axis, making their extension to the
tapered ends unnecessary.
4. Protection of the extreme dimensions: The keel must remain inside the moulded line of the bilge, so
that it does not increase the vessel's extreme breadth or draught. Carrying it forward or aft, where the hull
form narrows, would push it outside that line and expose it to grounding and quay contact — which is why it sits
at the turn of the bilge amidships.

E11.title: Roll reduction systems
E11.answer_markdown:
i) Bilge Keels: Bilge keels are narrow fins or plates attached amidships, longitudinally along the turn of the
bilge, where the bottom curves into the sides, on both sides. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance
when the vessel rolls, creating a damping effect that reduces the amplitude of rolling motions. The design
usually involves flat plates or strakes that present resistance to water flow during a roll, thus helping to stabilize
the vessel.
Stated precisely, bilge keels are a passive damping device and the damping is produced by eddy and vortex
shedding at the sharp edges of the keel: as the hull rolls, the keels are dragged through the water and shed
vortices, and the energy carried away in those vortices is taken out of the rolling motion, so the roll is damped.
Because the damping force depends on the velocity of the water relative to the keel, bilge keels oppose roll
velocity rather than roll displacement. They therefore bite hardest at resonance, where roll velocity is greatest,
and have little effect at zero speed or where there is no relative motion between hull and water. A roll-amplitude
reduction of approximately 20–35% is a useful figure to quote.

Original sketch — bilge keel at turn of bilge (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.6
Advantages:
• Low Maintenance: They require minimal maintenance compared to active stabilization systems.
• No Internal Components: Unlike fins or other stabilization systems, bilge keels do not take up space inside
the hull, preserving cargo and operational areas.
• Cost-Effective: They are relatively inexpensive to install and maintain.
Disadvantages:
• Increased Drag: The presence of bilge keels increases hydrodynamic resistance, which can reduce speed
and fuel efficiency.
• Limited Effectiveness: While they reduce roll, bilge keels are not as effective as other stabilization
methods like fins or gyroscopic stabilizers.
• Potential Damage: They can be susceptible to damage when docking or grounding as they protrude out
from the hull.
ii) Passive Uncontrolled Tanks: Passive uncontrolled tanks utilize the principles of fluid dynamics to reduce
roll by allowing water to move freely within tanks located in the hull. As the vessel rolls, water shifts from one
side of the tank to the other, creating a counteracting moment that helps stabilize the ship. This system does
not require active control or mechanical components.
The key marking point is the tuning principle. A passive uncontrolled tank — the free-surface or Frahm type —
works because the natural period of the water oscillating in the tank is tuned to the ship's natural
roll period. When correctly tuned, the moment generated by the moving water lags the roll by about 90°,
so that it opposes roll velocity and gives maximum damping near resonance. Omitting the phrase “tuned to the
ship's natural roll period” normally loses a mark. It follows that if the tank is mistuned, or the ship is
operating far from resonance, a free-surface tank can actually worsen the roll. Note also the
terminology: “passive uncontrolled” means the free-surface / Frahm type with no throttle valve, as
distinct from “passive controlled”, which has a tunable air cross-over or water-duct valve that adjusts the tank's
response.

Original sketch — passive (free-surface) anti-roll tank, athwartship view (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.7
Advantages:
• Simplicity: The system is straightforward with no moving parts, leading to lower maintenance requirements
and reduced failure points.
• Cost-Effective Installation: Passive tanks can be integrated into existing designs without significant
modifications or costs associated with active systems.
• Increased Stability: They provide an effective means of roll reduction by utilizing the natural movement of
water within the tanks.
Disadvantages:
• Delayed Response Time: The effectiveness of passive tanks can be slower than active systems since they
rely on fluid movement rather than immediate mechanical response.
• Reduced Stability (Free Surface Effect): The presence of a large, freely moving liquid surface inside the
tanks creates a free-surface effect, which decreases the ship's metacentric height and can reduce initial
stability. This loss of GM is unavoidable, precisely because the system depends on having a free surface.
• Significant Space Consumption: They occupy a large volume of the vessel's interior, often reducing
usable cargo or storage space.

E12.title: Double-bottom fuel tanks — sounding pipes, air pipes & vent design
E12.answer_markdown:
(a) Weighted cocks are fitted to tank sounding pipes for the following reasons:
• Preventing Water Ingress: The weighted design helps keep the cock closed when not in use, preventing
water from entering the tank through the sounding pipe, which could lead to contamination of the fuel.
• Ease of Operation: When the sounding pipe is needed for measuring liquid levels, the weight allows for
easy operation, ensuring that the cock can be opened and closed smoothly without requiring excessive force.
The cock is a self-closing weighted cock: the weight returns it to the shut position as soon as the hand is
taken off it, so the pipe cannot be left open. Describe the pipe itself as well — it runs from the tank top down to
a striking plate on the tank bottom, which takes the impact of the sounding rod, it terminates at an accessible
deck level at the cock, and it must be run as straight as practicable so that the rod or tape reaches the
bottom.
(b) Purpose of Air Pipes:
• Pressure Equalization: They allow air to flow in and out of the tank, preventing pressure build-up or
vacuum formation as fuel is pumped in or out. This ensures safe and efficient operation during filling and
emptying.
• Ventilation: Air pipes help ventilate the tank, allowing any gases that may accumulate to escape, thus
reducing the risk of explosive atmospheres within the tank.
The sizing rule follows from the first purpose: the air-pipe cross-sectional area must be at least 1.25 times the
area of the filling line, so that the vent can never become the restriction during bunkering and over-
pressurise the tank.
(c) Design Features Incorporated on Air Pipe Vents
• i. Heavy Weather: Air pipes are often designed with a gooseneck shape, which helps prevent water from
entering the pipe during heavy seas. The upward bend creates a barrier against wave action. The head is
fitted with a float-type automatic self-closing device, which shuts if the vent is submerged by a boarding
sea. Under the Load Line Convention the coaming height before the automatic closing device must be
at least 760 mm on the freeboard deck and 450 mm on the superstructure deck.
• ii. Fire: Air pipes are equipped with flame arresters to prevent flames from entering the tank in case of an
external fire, thereby reducing the risk of explosion due to flammable vapors inside the tank. In practice this
is a corrosion-resistant flame screen fitted in the vent head, removable for cleaning.
• iii. Bunkering: For safety during bunkering operations, fuel tank air vents are fitted with suitable sized save-
all trays around the base of air pipe. Vents are located at the highest point of the tank to prevent air pockets
and terminate on open decks. They allow air to flow out of the tank, preventing pressure build-up as fuel is
pumped in. This ensures safe and efficient bunkering. The 1.25 × filling-line area rule applies here, and
the vent must terminate clear of accommodation openings and of any source of ignition.
Quoting the coaming heights and the 1.25 × area rule is what lifts this part from a descriptive answer to a
specification-level one.

E31.title: Construction of refrigerated spaces — insulation materials, properties & attachment
E31.answer_markdown:
a) Suitable materials that can be used for insulation refrigerated spaces are; (i) Cork · (ii) Fiber Glass · (iii)
Mineral Wool · (iv) Foam. Modern practice is dominated by closed-cell rigid foams — polyurethane (PUF)
and polyisocyanurate (PIR), often supplied as factory-bonded panels; cork, glass-fibre and mineral wool are
the traditional materials. Naming a closed-cell foam by name is worth doing, because it is what is actually fitted
in a modern reefer space.
b) Properties that an insulating material should process are;
• It should have low thermal conductivity.
• It should resistance to mold and vermin.
• Resistance to moisture.
• It should be non-hazardous/toxic.
• It should be non-corrosive.
• It should be noncombustible.
• It must incorporate a vapour / moisture barrier — the property most often left out, and the one that
matters most.
• It must be dimensionally stable, of low water-absorption, odourless, rot- and vermin-proof, light, and fire-
retardant.
The vapour barrier is essential because condensation forming on the cold side and wetting the insulation
destroys its insulating value: a wet insulant conducts, so the R-value collapses and the space cannot hold
temperature. The sealing strips and the sheet-metal facing in the sketch below are there for exactly this
purpose — they are the vapour seal, not merely a finish.
c) Cross-section of a wall of cold storage space:

Cold-storage wall section — insulation attachment to ship structure (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.12
The insulation is not fastened to the shell or the frames directly. Wood grounds are secured to the structure by
lugs welded to the frames; the insulation is laid between and against the grounds, the joints are closed with
sealing strips, and the whole is faced with sheet metal on the cold side, which both protects the insulant
mechanically and completes the vapour seal.

E32.title: Double hulled oil tankers — mid-ship section, why they evolved & the disadvantages
E32.answer_markdown:
Sol: a)
Double-hull oil tanker — mid-ship cross section (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.10
Working outwards from the centre line the section shows the keel strake and centre girder, the double
bottom with its floors, side girders and inner bottom shell, the bilge strake turning up into the side shell and
the inner shell that together form the wing water ballast tanks, the longitudinal bulkhead dividing the port
and starboard cargo tanks, and at deck level the deck plating, deck stringer plate and sheer strake with
the horizontal girders, end brackets and plate brackets that tie the inner and outer skins together.
b) Double-hulled oil tankers evolved over a period of time to minimize massive oil spills resulting from
groundings, collisions or internal tank rupturing. Following catastrophic accidents like the Exxon Valdez,
international regulations (MARPOL) and US law (OPA 90) mandated this design because the extra, protective
inner layer prevents cargo tank rupture during lower-impact incidents. The requirement is MARPOL Annex I,
Regulation 19, which requires double-hull or equivalent construction for oil tankers, with the phase-out of
existing single-hull tankers under Regulation 20. The United States driver is OPA 90, following the 1989
Exxon Valdez grounding.

c) Dis-Advantages of this type of design are;
1. Explosion and atmosphere risk in the double-hull void spaces. The narrow voids between the
skins can accumulate hydrocarbon vapour leaking from the cargo tanks, and they must therefore be
inerted or ventilated and routinely gas-monitored — the lesson of the Bow Mariner.
2. Increased Construction and Operational Costs.
3. Difficult Maintenance and Inspections. Access for close-up survey in the narrow ballast voids is poor, and
the incidence of corrosion in them is high, so coating condition has to be maintained in the least
accessible part of the ship.
4. Increased light weight of the vessel. The additional steel weight is a real penalty because it is deducted
from deadweight, so for a given displacement the ship carries less cargo.
5. Reduced Stability and High Center of Gravity.
6. The cost of coating and maintaining the additional ballast spaces over the life of the ship.
If only four disadvantages are wanted, give the atmosphere risk in the voids, the survey access and corrosion in
the narrow ballast spaces, the steel weight lost from deadweight, and the coating and maintenance cost of the
extra tanks — those four are the technically defensible set.
Source note: Part 2 lists the four disadvantages as increased cost, difficult maintenance and inspection, increased light weight,
and “Reduced Stability and High Center of Gravity”, and its own Model Additions box then records that the “increased light
weight → reduced stability / high CG” reasoning is loosely argued and tells the candidate to lead with the void-space atmosphere
risk, the survey access and corrosion, the deadweight penalty and the coating cost instead. All four original items are preserved
above; the stronger items have been added and put first, and the light-weight point is re-expressed as a deadweight penalty,
which is what it actually is.

E33.title: Large bulk carriers — mid-ship section & the design features that resist
E33.answer_markdown:
Sol: a)
Large bulk carrier — mid-ship cross section (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.32
The section is the classic single-side-skin bulker: a duct keel and double bottom tank with centre girder and
floors, the hopper tank with its sloping plating and transverse ring webs carrying the load out to the bilge, the
side shell with side-shell frames and longitudinals, and the topside tank with its sloping plating, vertical
strake and transverse ring web running up to the strength deck and the hatch coaming. The topside and

hopper tanks are what give the section both its strength and its self-trimming geometry: the sloping plating
makes the cargo flow to the centre, and the tanks themselves are the ballast capacity.
b) To minimise the possibility of failure in large bulk carriers, several key design features have evolved by
Utilization of corrugated transverse bulkheads which enhances strength by effectively distributing stress during
operations and at sea. Transverse watertight bulkheads between cargo holds prevent flooding from spreading,
increasing survivability in emergencies. Implementing alternate hold loading helps distribute cargo weight
evenly, reducing stress on the hull and maintaining stability. Water ingress alarms alert crews to rising water
levels in cargo holds, enabling prompt action to prevent flooding. Adoption of double hulls provides an extra
layer of protection against leaks and breaches, significantly improving safety.
These features are the SOLAS Chapter XII bulk-carrier safety measures, introduced after the heavy bulk-
carrier losses of the 1980s and 1990s — the Derbyshire era. Named individually they are:
• Mandatory water-ingress detection alarms in the cargo holds and in the forward spaces.
• A strengthened No.1 hold and, above all, a strengthened transverse corrugated bulkhead between
Nos. 1 and 2 holds — the critical interface, because it is failure there that turns flooding of No.1 hold into
progressive flooding of the ship.
• Loading-instrument verification, with restricted or alternate-hold loading, to keep shear force and
bending moment inside the permissible envelope during multi-port loading and discharge.
• The move to double-side-skin construction, which removes the exposed side-shell frames and their end
brackets — a known wastage and fracture site on single-side-skin ships.

E34.title: Bulk carrier — inspection of the upper topside areas as Chief Engineer
E34.answer_markdown:
As Chief Engineer Officer on a bulk carrier, inspection of the upper topside areas is crucial for structural
integrity, safety, and operational efficiency. Inspection regime focuses on mitigating corrosion, ensuring
watertight integrity, and structural reliability as follows;
i) Hatch Covers and Coamings: Inspect for cracks, deformation, and wastage, especially at the corners of
hatches, which are high-stress areas.
ii) Watertight Integrity: Check the condition of rubber gaskets, packing, and sealing arrangements for all
hatch covers.
iii) Securing Devices: Ensure all hatch cleats, hinges, and quick-acting cleats are operational and well-
greased.
iv) Air Pipes & Sounding Pipes: Inspect the air pipes to the topside tanks for corrosion, particularly in the
threads, and verify the proper functioning to prevent water ingress. Confirm in particular that the automatic
(float-type) closing devices on the topside tank air pipes are free and seating — a seized or missing float is a
direct route to progressive flooding of the topside tanks.
v) Deck Structures: Check for wasting or pitting on deck plating, particularly around crane foundations,
pedestal mounts, and windlasses. Include the cross-deck strips between hatches and the hatch-end
beams, which carry the transverse deck loading between the hatch openings.
vi) Ventilation and Access: Ensure the manholes, ladders, and ventilation access to the tanks are safe, clean,
and not compromised.
vii) Underside of Upper Deck: Inspect for buckling or corrosion of deck stiffeners. Extend this into the
topside (sloping) tank internal structure and its brackets, which is the structure this question is really
about — the sloping plating, its longitudinals, the transverse ring webs and the bracket toes where they land.
viii) Load line marks: Ensure the load line marks and draft marks are clearly visible and not obstructed by
corrosion or paint. Confirm that the markings have not been altered and are still compliant with regulatory
standards.
ix) Fire Fighting System Check: Inspect the condition of fire hoses, nozzles, and sprinkler systems for
readiness and compliance with regulations.
x) Lighting: Verify that emergency lighting and work lighting in the upper deck spaces are functioning.
xi) The bulk-carrier-specific structure
Two further items turn a general deck inspection into a bulk-carrier inspection, and both should be named. First,
the transverse corrugated bulkheads and their lower stools between holds, inspected from the topside
tanks and hold access — this is the classic No.1 / No.2 hold progressive-flooding failure mode, where a corroded
or buckled corrugation lets flooding of one hold into the next. Second, on a single-side-skin bulker, the side-
shell frames and their end brackets at the top and bottom connections, a known wastage hotspot where
grab damage, alternate wetting and coating breakdown combine.

E35.title: Transverse watertight bulkheads — reasons, what constitutes one, minimum number & testing
E35.answer_markdown:
a) Transverse watertight bulkheads in ship construction serve several critical purposes:
• Flooding Prevention: They divide the ship into separate compartments, helping to contain flooding in the
event of a hull breach, limiting the spread of water and enhancing survivability.
• Structural Integrity: They contribute to the overall structural strength, helping resist bending and shear
forces that occur during operations, particularly in rough seas.
• Stability Improvement: By providing additional support and reducing free surface effects, they help
enhance the ship's stability.
• Fire Containment: They can serve as fire barriers, restricting the spread of fire from one compartment to
another.
The second printing of the same question puts the same three reasons more tightly, and this is the form to write
if only three are asked for: Reasons for Fitting Transverse Watertight Bulkheads: Flood Prevention
(compartmentalize the ship, limiting water ingress if the hull is breached, maintaining buoyancy and stability);
Structural Integrity (provide strength, acting as pillars supporting deck and tank tops); Fire Containment (slow
the spread of flames and smoke between compartments).
What constitutes a watertight bulkhead
A watertight bulkhead is a vertical partition within a ship designed to prevent water ingress into adjacent
compartments. It must be constructed with minimal openings, able to withstand hydrostatic pressure when
flooded, with reinforced plating (steel or equivalent) to ensure integrity under pressure. In practice that means
plating stiffened vertically or horizontally and scantled for the design head of water — the head to the
bulkhead deck — with every penetration made good: watertight doors of an approved class, cable and pipe
penetrations sealed by approved glands, and no unprotected openings below the bulkhead deck.
b) The minimum number of transverse watertight bulkheads typically required includes:
• Collision Bulkhead: Located at the forward end, designed to protect against collision damage, extending
from the bottom of the hull to the upper deck. Its position is set by rule: not less than 0.05 L and not more
than 0.08 L abaft the forward perpendicular — in some cases 0.05 L + 3 m — which is the figure that earns
the mark.
• After Peak Bulkhead: Situated at the aft end, enclosing the stern tube, extending to at least the first deck
above the load waterline.
• Machinery Space Bulkheads: A watertight bulkhead is required at each end of the machinery space.
Stated as a count: Minimum Number and Location: One Collision Bulkhead (forward); One Aft Peak Bulkhead
(stern); One Bulkhead at Each End of the Engine Room. So for a ship with machinery amidships the
minimum is typically four transverse watertight bulkheads — collision, after peak, and one at each end of the
machinery space — while an aft-machinery ship needs a minimum of three, because the after-peak
bulkhead and the after machinery-space bulkhead can be one and the same. Above that minimum the number
required increases with ship length under the class rules, and for a ship carrying passengers it is set by the
floodable-length and damage-stability calculation rather than by a count.

c) The second printing answers this as: Testing: Pressure Testing (hose simulating water pressure to check for
leaks and structural integrity); Visual Inspection (for buckling or deformation); Air Leak Testing (pressurized air
within a compartment to detect leaks by monitoring air escape). That list conflates two different tests under
“pressure testing”, so set them out separately, because they prove different things.
• Hose Test: A hose test involves applying water pressure to check for leaks. Water is sprayed or directed
onto the bulkhead's surface, ensuring that no water seeps through any joints or connections. What this
proves is joint and seam tightness only — it says nothing about the strength of the bulkhead.
• Fill (head) test: the proper strength and boundary test is to fill the compartment to the head the bulkhead
is designed for, so that the test reproduces the design hydrostatic head and the structure is loaded as it
would be in the flooded condition.
• Air / leak test: where filling is impracticable, pressurise the compartment with air to the approved test
pressure and paint the seams with a leak-indicating solution, which shows a leak as bubbles. Air Leak
Testing (pressurized air within a compartment to detect leaks by monitoring air escape).
• Visual Inspection (for buckling or deformation) accompanies whichever test is used, before and after.
Source note: Part 2 answers this topic twice. At p.30 part (c) is answered with the hose test alone, and its Model Additions box
records that a hose test proves joint and seam tightness only, the proper strength test being a fill (head) test to the design head
or an air test with leak-indicating solution. At p.48 part (d) is printed as “Pressure Testing (hose simulating water pressure to

E36.title: Aluminium alloy in shipbuilding — advantages, disadvantages & welding of
E36.answer_markdown:
a) Advantage: (i) Light weight (ii) Corrosion resistance (iii) High versatility (iv) Recyclability.
Dis-Advantages: (i) Softer than steel (ii) Expensive (iii) Corrodes rapidly in sea water (iv) Requires specialised
welding techniques. Two further disadvantages actually govern the design: aluminium's low melting point
and loss of strength in a fire, which is why an aluminium structure forming a fire division has to be insulated
to the A-class standard on the basis that the core temperature must not rise to the point where the alloy loses
strength; and its higher coefficient of thermal expansion than steel, roughly twice that of steel, which has
to be allowed for at joints and at aluminium-to-steel connections.
The corrosion behaviour needs stating correctly. Aluminium forms a self-protecting oxide film and is in
general corrosion-resistant in seawater — better than mild steel. The real problem is galvanic corrosion at
aluminium-to-steel joints, where the aluminium is anodic to the steel and wastes rapidly; such joints must be
electrically isolated with insulating material or made through an explosion-bonded bi-metallic transition
strip, so that the aluminium is welded to aluminium and the steel to steel.
b)
TIG (gas tungsten arc) welding (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.26
Gas tungsten arc welding is referred to as "TIG" welding. It utilizes a non-consumable tungsten electrode and
separate filler metal in the form of a wire (not used for thin sections). Inert shielding gas is supplied through an
annular nozzle around the tungsten electrode. It is better suited for shop fabrication than field fabrication
because movement must be less than 5 mph to maintain the inert gas blanket. The consumable filler metal is

added either manually or by some mechanized process. The inert gas shielding protects the molten metal,
which is cooling, and it also provides the required arc characteristics.
The process may use direct current (DC), with positive or negative polarity, attached to the tungsten electrode,
although in most applications the electrode is attached to the negative polarity. Alternative current (AC) is also
used to produce different effects on the welding. Argon and helium are the two inert gases used for this process.
Choice of gas and type of current and polarity depends on the type of material and quality of weld desired.
Applied to aluminium specifically
For aluminium the choice is AC TIG (or AC MIG), and the reason should be given: the cathodic half-cycle of the
alternating current breaks up the tenacious oxide film, which melts at a far higher temperature than the
parent metal and would otherwise remain as an inclusion in the weld. The joint must be cleaned and the
oxide mechanically removed immediately before welding, and pre-heat and interpass temperature
must be controlled to avoid porosity — hydrogen is very soluble in molten aluminium — and lack-of-fusion
defects, aluminium's high thermal conductivity carrying heat away from the joint. Argon is the usual shielding
gas; helium, or an argon-helium mixture, gives a hotter arc and deeper penetration for thicker sections.
Source note: Part 2's original list gives “Corrodes rapidly in sea water” as a disadvantage, and its own Model Additions box
records that this is misleading — aluminium forms a self-protecting oxide film and is generally corrosion-resistant, the real
problem being galvanic corrosion at aluminium-to-steel joints. The original item is preserved above as printed and the corrected
mechanism is given immediately after it, so the galvanic explanation is what gets written in the exam.

E38.title: Roll reduction — bilge keels plus TWO other methods, with advantages & disadvantages
E38.answer_markdown:
a) Bilge Keels: Bilge keels are narrow fins or plates attached amidships, longitudinally along the turn of the
bilge, where the bottom curves into the sides, on both sides. They work by increasing hydrodynamic resistance
when the vessel rolls, creating a damping effect that reduces the amplitude of rolling motions. The design
usually involves flat plates or strakes that present resistance to water flow during a roll, thus helping to stabilize
the vessel.
Advantages: Low Maintenance (require minimal maintenance compared to active stabilization systems) · No
Internal Components (do not take up space inside the hull, preserving cargo and operational areas) · Cost-
Effective (relatively inexpensive to install and maintain). They also work at any speed, including zero speed
and at anchor, because the damping comes from the ship's own rolling velocity and not from forward way.
b) Other methods of roll reduction are;
i) Anti Roll Tanks: Passive uncontrolled tanks utilize the principles of fluid dynamics to reduce roll by allowing
water to move freely within tanks located in the hull. As the vessel rolls, water shifts from one side of the tank to
the other, creating a counteracting moment that helps stabilize the ship. This system does not require active
control or mechanical components. The effect depends on the water arriving out of phase with the roll, so
the tank and its cross-over duct are tuned to the ship's natural roll period; if that period changes with
loading — that is, with a change of GM — the tank can become ineffective, or in the worst case can arrive in
phase and amplify the roll. Advantages: Simplicity · Cost-Effective Installation · effective roll damping close to
the natural roll period, and at zero speed. Disadvantages: Delayed Response Time · Reduced Stability (Free
Surface Effect) · Significant Space Consumption. To those add the tuning dependence just described.
(ii) Active Fin Stabilizers: Fin stabilizers are underwater, wing-like appendages attached to both sides of a
ship's hull below the waterline that reduce roll motion caused by waves. They work like wings, using sensors to
tilt the fins, creating hydraulic lift that acts against the wave-induced rolling motion. When a ship rolls, sensors
detect the movement and command hydraulic cylinders to tilt the fins, creating counter-acting upward or
downward forces. Advantages: Superior Roll Reduction · Enhanced Safety and Comfort · Highly efficient at
reducing roll at higher, cruising speeds. Disadvantages: Increased Drag and Fuel Consumption · Risk of
Damage and Vulnerability · Space Limitations. And, the standard counterpoint, they are ineffective at low
speed and at anchor, because a fin can only generate lift with water flowing past it. That is the comparison
the question is looking for: bilge keels and passive tanks work at zero speed, fins do not; fins are far more
effective than either once the ship is up to service speed.
Source note: Part 2's original answer lists “Increased Stability” among the advantages of the passive anti-roll tank and
“Reduced Stability (Free Surface Effect)” among its disadvantages, and its own Model Additions box records that this is
contradictory and instructs that “Increased Stability” be removed: a passive tank does not increase stability, its free surface
always reduces GM, and the genuine benefit is roll-amplitude damping near the natural roll period at a small GM cost. That is the
one place in this entry where original wording has been changed rather than added to — the advantage now reads “effective roll
damping close to the natural roll period, and at zero speed”. The disadvantage is preserved as printed.

E13.title: Watertight / weathertight doors · bilge injection valve
E13.answer_markdown:
(a) (i) Watertight doors: Watertight doors on ships are critical safety barriers designed to prevent the spread
of flooding between compartments during emergencies, limiting the spread of water within the vessel and help
maintain its buoyancy and stability. The defining requirement is that the door withstands a static head of
water from either side without leakage, and it is designed for the pressure at its particular location, that
pressure being set by the subdivision and damage-stability calculation for the ship.
They are essential in any opening that compromises the watertight integrity of the ship's hull, ensuring that
water does not flow between compartments during emergencies. These doors are installed below the
bulkhead (freeboard) deck, in areas prone to flooding such as: Shaft tunnels · Ballast tanks · Engine room
bulkheads · Pipe tunnels.
ii) Weathertight Doors: Weathertight doors are designed to withstand weather conditions and prevent water
from entering the vessel during heavy seas or rain. They can withstand brief submersion and provide fire and
smoke containment, enhancing overall safety. The definition to give is that water will not penetrate into the
ship in any sea condition — achieved by gaskets and cleats — but that the door is not designed to hold a
sustained head of water, which is the essential difference from a watertight door.
They are critical for maintaining the ship's integrity against environmental conditions without compromising
internal safety features. These doors are installed on the freeboard (weather) deck and in
superstructures, in areas subjected to adverse weather conditions such as: Main Decks · Accommodation
Entrances · Navigation Bridge Entrances · Engine Room Entrance.
(b) A bilge injection valve is incorporated into the main sea water system to provide emergency bilge pumping
capacity, allowing large main sea water pumps to directly remove high volumes of floodwater from the engine
room in situations like collision or grounding. It is a normally closed, non-return valve, often with a red handle,
connected to the suction side of the main cooling pump. Specifically it is a screw-down non-return (SDNR)
valve, fitted on the suction of the largest-capacity sea-water (main circulating) pump, with a diameter
typically not less than two-thirds of the main sea suction, and with the handwheel mounted high and
readily accessible above the anticipated flood level. This arrangement gives the maximum possible emergency
dewatering capacity for the machinery space.
Testing is performed to ensure operation, through the following steps:
1. Preparation: Place a screen over the strainer at the bilge injection suction point to prevent debris from
entering the pump, while ensuring the area is relatively clear. Make arrangements for the suction at the bilge
injection valve.
2. Procedure: Open the bilge injection valve. Ensure the valve operates freely and the spindle is in good
condition.
3. Operation: Start the main sea water pump and close the main sea chest (sea inlet) valve to create suction
from the bilge.

4. Verification: Monitor the pressure gauges to ensure suction is working and check that water is being
discharged overboard.
5. Completion: Once tested, close the bilge injection valve and re-open the main sea chest to restore normal
cooling water flow. After successful testing record the test results in the logbook. After testing replace the seal
on the valve. State the safety caution as part of the answer: the valve must never be left cracked open in
service, because if the non-return element passes, the sea will flood the bilge. Confirm that it shuts tight on
completion of the test.
Source note: Part 1 locates the two door types “below” and “above the waterline”. Its Model Additions record that this is only
loosely right; the precise boundary is the freeboard (bulkhead) deck, and that wording is used above.

E14.title: Watertight-door classification, closure & safe passage
E14.answer_markdown:
a) Watertight bulkhead access doors are classified as follows:
• Type A: These doors may be left open and are to be closed only during emergencies.
• Type B: These doors should remain closed but can be opened when personnel are working in the adjacent
compartment.
• Type C: These doors must remain closed at all times, only opening briefly when personnel pass through.
• Type D: These doors shall be closed before the voyage commences and shall be kept closed during
navigation.
That is the operational usage classification, taken from the IMO MSC.1 circular on the operation of watertight
doors. Because the question could equally be read as asking about the construction classification, state both:
SOLAS II-1 separately classifies watertight doors by operating type — Class 1 hinged, Class 2 hand-operated
sliding, and Class 3 power-operated sliding, closeable from the bridge. Giving both schemes covers either
reading of the question.
b) Circumstances under which all watertight doors must be closed when situations are defined as potentially
hazardous are;
• Heavy weather conditions or where depth is less than 3 times the draught.
• Proximity to underwater hazards, port limits or compulsory pilotage waters.
• Restricted visibility, high traffic density or any other factor constituting a hazard.
c) Procedure to pass safely through a hydraulically operated watertight door;
• The door is hydraulically operated and has three operating positions, bridge control, emergency position, and
local control. Locate Controls, Check Indicators, and move the local handle to the 'open' position and wait
until the door is completely open.

• Before opening, confirm that the bridge master mode switch is set to “local control”. If it is set to
“doors closed” — as it will be during a drill or an emergency — the door will re-close as soon as the local
handle is released, which is a crushing hazard. Check both the local and the remote open/closed indicators.
• Pass quickly and safely, watching your footing using the handles provided on the door to assist in movement.
• After passing through, move the local handle to the 'close' position to close the door until the green light
indicates.
• Never attempt to pass through a door while it is moving (risk of fatal crush injuries) and never stop a closing
door. Emphasize the need to keep doors closed at sea for water tight integrity.
• After the explanation, physically demonstrate the operation of a hydraulically operated watertight door and
ensure the crew member can operate it safely.
Where the sitting instead asks for the safety features designed into the operating system, present the
same material as design provisions: audible alarm before and during travel, local and bridge open/closed
indicators, a hold-to-run local handle on both sides of the bulkhead, controlled closing time and closing
force, and an independent power supply so the door remains operable on loss of main power.

E15.title: Watertight doors — number/size factors, operating requirements & hazards
E15.answer_markdown:
(a) Factors that affect the number and size of watertight doors compatible with the proper working of the ship
are;
1. Subdivision and Damage Stability Requirements (Safety Factor): A (singular) watertight door is
required where a watertight bulkhead requires access through it for passage.
2. Operational Function and Access Requirements (Functional Factor): WTDs are restricted to essential
access points (shaft tunnel, duct keel, passage between compartments for passengers on passenger ships). The
size of the opening shall be made as small as possible.
3. Structural Strength of the Bulkhead (Structural Factor): The number and size of WTDs must be limited
to allow for proper framing and structural reinforcement of the bulkhead to maintain its strength against water
pressure.
b) Operating requirements of watertight doors below the weather deck are;
1. Safety and Emergency Power: WTDs must be kept closed at sea, used only for passage, and immediately
closed after. WTDs should have two sources of power, including an independent, emergency power source to
ensure operation during a blackout. A power-operated sliding door has its own hydraulic accumulator or
independent power supply, sufficient for at least three complete open-and-close cycles against a 15°
list with no main power available, corresponding to about an hour of independent operation.
2. Remote Closure & Local Control: Must be capable of being closed simultaneously from the bridge within
60 seconds, with the ship listed up to 15°. Must be operable locally from both sides of the bulkhead. The two
closure times must be kept separate, and this is the most commonly lost mark on this question: the 60
seconds is the time to close all doors simultaneously from the bridge master switch, whereas an
individual power-operated sliding door must close in 20 to 40 seconds with the ship upright when it is
operated on its own. The bridge also carries a master mode switch, selecting “local control” or “doors
closed”.
3. Alarms & Indicators: Remote, audible alarms must sound for 10 seconds before and during closure.
Remote, visual, “open/closed” indicators must be present at the bridge and control station. These figures are
those of SOLAS II-1 Regulations 13 and 13-1, and quoting the regulation earns credit.
c) Potential hazards when passing through power operated watertight doors are;
1. Crushing Injuries/Fatalities: The doors close with immense force, sufficient to crush bones or cause fatal
injuries if a person is caught in between while it is already in motion.
2. Hand/Body Safety Risks: Sliding WTDs are often moved by hydraulic cylinders and can cause severe
injuries if hands or clothing are caught in the pinch points.
3. Sudden Automatic Re-closure: If a WTD is opened locally while the master mode switch on the bridge is
set to “closed” (e.g., during a drill or emergency), the door will immediately close upon release of the local
handle.
4. Lack of Situational Awareness: In noisy environments, the audio-visual alarms may go unnoticed or
unheard.
Potential hazards could be eliminated by;

1. Adherence to alarm systems, standard operating procedure and clear signage.
2. Mandatory two-handed manual operation (hold-to-open local handle procedure).
3. Prohibition of carrying load alone and passing while door is in motion.
4. Regular training and familiarization.
Source note: Part 1's part (b) quotes only the 60-second bridge closure. Its Model Additions require the 20–40 second
individual door closing time to be added, and it has been folded into point 2 above.

E16.title: Conditions of assignment of load line
E16.answer_markdown:
To ensure compliance with load line assignment according to The International Convention on Load Lines, 1966
(ICLL 1966) and The UK Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Regulations 1998, inspections focus on maintaining the
vessel's watertight/weathertight integrity, structural strength, and crew safety. Key items include closing
appliances (hatches, doors), air pipes, ventilators, scuppers, side scuttles, cargo ports, and marking of the deck
line and load lines. Critical inspection areas for load line compliance are;
i) Load Line Markings: The deck line, load line marks, and draught marks must be clearly visible, painted, and
properly located, and must agree with the freeboard shown on the certificate.
ii) Hatchways and Closures: All hatch covers on exposed decks must be weathertight, with secured closing
appliances, tarpaulins, and securing devices.
iii) Machinery Space Openings: Openings on freeboard decks must have efficient weathertight closures.
Engine room skylights and fiddley openings must be in good condition.
iv) Manholes and Flush Scuttles: Must be watertight and capable of being secured.
v) Ventilators and Air Pipes: All ventilators (including air pipe closing devices) must be efficient,
weathertight, and capable of being closed.
vi) Side Scuttles and Deadlights: Below the freeboard deck must be watertight, including checking packing
for cracks.
vii) Cargo Ports and Watertight Doors: All openings in the ship's side below the freeboard deck must be
securely watertight.
viii) Scuppers, Inlets, and Discharges: Non-return valves on overboard discharges must be functional and
effective.

ix) Bulwarks and Guardrails: Must be structurally sound, secure, and maintained in good condition to protect
the crew and allow drainage.
x) Structure and Stability: General structural integrity of the hull, frame, and bulkheads, along with
documentation of stability, must be verified.
xi) Freeing ports in bulwarks: The freeing-port area must be correct for the length of bulwark served, and
the non-return flaps must be free to operate and not seized, painted up or lashed. This is a classic conditions-of-
assignment item.
xii) Protection of the crew and means of access: Guard rails, lifelines, gangways and walkways, and the
safe access arrangements between the accommodation and the machinery space. These are expressly an ICLL
condition of assignment, not merely good practice.
xiii) Coaming heights and positions: Hatch, ventilator and air-pipe coamings must be of the required height
for their position, distinguishing Position 1 from Position 2, together with the required companionway and
door sill heights.
Finally, tie the inspection back to the documents, which is what converts a list of items into a proper conditions-
of-assignment answer. The assigned marks must agree with the freeboard shown on a valid Load Line
Certificate; the certificate and the stability book must be checked; and it must be confirmed that no
structural alteration has been made that would change the assigned freeboard. On an older, newly
purchased vessel these three checks are the priority.

E39.title: Hydraulically operated folding hatch cover — operation, watertightness & security
E39.answer_markdown:
Sol: (a)
Hydraulically operated folding hatch cover (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.24
The Hatch cover sketched is made of a pair of covers operated by a hydraulic cylinder for opening and closing.
The cylinder is connected to the first hatch cover at one end and is secured to the deck at the other end. The
pressurisation and de-pressurisation of the cylinder causes the first cover to move. The first cover is connected
to the second using a roller arrangement and chain track which helps in transfer of motion for opening and
closing. The chain track also acts as a guide. When closing a part of the rail can be retracted so that the end
wheel is lowered down causing the neoprene seal to press down on the coming rail.
Read in order, then: extending the cylinder lifts the leading pair of panels about their hinge so that the two
panels fold face to face and travel along the coaming top on their end wheels in the chain track, stowing
vertically at the hatch end. Closing reverses it — the folded pair runs back along the track, and at the end of
travel the retractable section of rail drops the end wheels so that the panels come down flat and the neoprene
seal is compressed onto the coaming rail rather than being dragged along it. Wheels off the rail and the cover
resting on its landing pads is what makes the seal work; the cleats then hold it there.
(b) The watertight integrity and security of a hatch cover can be done by carrying out cheks of the cleat
arrangement which helps in securing the hatch on the cover. Before securing of the cleat we need to ensure the

Neoprene seal is properly seated on the coaming rail. Before proceeding to sea, and because this part carries 3
marks in its own right, go further:
• Ascertain tightness by a hose test at not less than 2 bar at the nozzle, or by an ultrasonic tightness
test of the perimeter seal, which gives a quantitative reading and can be done with cargo loaded and in any
weather.
• Confirm the rubber-to-compression-bar contact by chalk or witness line all round, and confirm that the
compression is correct — the rubber compressed onto the bar but not over-compressed or permanently "set",
since a set gasket cannot recover and will leak.
• Check that the drainage channels and the non-return drain valves in the coaming are clear, so that
any water passing the first barrier drains overboard instead of into the hold.
• Verify that all cleats, cross-joint wedges and the locating and landing pads are correctly set and
bearing, so that the cover cannot lift, shift or "pant" against its seal in a seaway.
Source note: Part 2 reproduces this answer with “cheks” for checks and “coming rail” for coaming rail, and records both as
spelling slips in its own note rather than editing the answer. They are left exactly as printed here for the same reason, since the
original answer text is not altered; both words are spelled correctly everywhere else in the entry.
