E40.title: Cargo hatch covers on large container ships — tightness testing, load transfer & wear
E40.answer_markdown:
a) Cargo hatch cover can be tested for water tightness by Hose test. In this test, a water spray from a nozzle of
12 mm diameter is sprayed over the joint of hold and cover from a distance of 1 m to 1.5 m with a pressure of
0.5 m/sec water jet. Any leak of water inside the cargo hold will indicate a gap between the hold and the cover.
The figures to quote are: nozzle bore not less than 12 mm, held not more than 1.5 m from the joint, water
pressure not less than 2 bar at the nozzle, and the jet traversed slowly along the whole length of the joint.
Other methods include: Chalk test (on top of bar that the hatch sealing rubber rests) · Ultrasonic testers ·
Inspect from inside of the closed hatch for any light penetrating. Of those, the chalk test only checks that
the rubber is being compressed onto the bar — it shows the contact line, but it does not prove tightness,
and it is not accepted as a tightness test. The definitive alternatives to the hose test are an ultrasonic
tightness test, which is preferred at sea because it gives a quantitative leak reading, is independent of the
weather and can be carried out with the hold loaded, and a pressure or vacuum test where the covers are
fitted for it.
b) Weight of lift-away pontoon type hatch cover and containers is transferred to ships structure using weight
bearing pads which are fitted to hatch coaming & hatch cover to relieve stress on elastomeric neoprene seal.
These support pads are designed to distribute heavy loads from container stacks evenly to the vessel's deck
structure. The bearing pads are not locked rigidly across the entire length; they are designed as separate, local
supports that allow the hatch cover to move slightly relative to the coaming without damaging the structure
during deflections of the hull in a seaway.
The principle worth stating explicitly is that the load path and the sealing path are kept separate: the
pads carry the vertical container load into the coaming and deck structure, while the neoprene seal carries no
load at all and only has to remain in compression. Because the hull works in a seaway — hogging, sagging and
twisting — the cover must be free to move a little relative to the coaming; the pads therefore locate it vertically
while the stoppers take the horizontal load, and nothing is rigidly built in.
c)

Hatch-cover support — weight-bearing pads, cleat, neoprene seal, coaming (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.19
1. Hatch Support Pads (Bearing Pads): Location — the interface between the hatch cover (bottom) and the
hatch coaming (top). Damage — excessive wear of steel or specialty pads (elastomeric or copper alloy) due to
the heavy loads of stacked containers and vessel vibration; this leads to reduced pad height, improper seating
of the hatch cover, uneven distribution of weight and potential stress cracks in surrounding steelwork.
2. Hatch Cover Stoppers (Restraining Devices): Location — longitudinal and transverse stoppers fitted at
the sides and ends of the hatch cover and coaming. Damage — wear and deformation of the stopper plates due
to constant buffeting of the cover during ship motion, causing enlarged clearances, allowing the hatch cover to
move, resulting in severe deformation of the stoppers and surrounding plate structure.
3. Hatch Cover Sealing Arrangement (Periphery): Location — the rubber gasket and the compression bar
(landing bar) on the coaming. Damage — improper support causes the sealing rubber to be compressed
unevenly, resulting in permanent deformation, hardening, or tearing of the seal; the compression bar itself can
show localized thinning due to corrosion and friction.
The three are one chain of consequences, and saying so is what earns the last mark: pads wear down, the cover
sits lower, the rubber is over-compressed and takes a permanent set, the cover then works against its stoppers,
and the enlarged clearances let it move further still — so worn pads are found as a leaking hatch and as
cracking in the coaming steelwork, not as a pad defect.
Source note: Part 2's original part (a) gives the hose test as “a pressure of 0.5 m/sec water jet”, and its own Model Additions
box records that 0.5 m/sec is a velocity and not a pressure, the markable figures being a nozzle of at least 12 mm held within
1.5 m at a water pressure of at least 2 bar. The original sentence is preserved above exactly as printed and the correct set of
figures follows it.

E41.title: Drainage from the external structure — scuppers, freeing ports & tanker handrails
E41.answer_markdown:
a) Scuppers are located in close proximity to the superstructure to instantly drain water away from weathertight
doors and vertical structures to prevent structural damage or flooding. Superstructures create corners and
obstructions where water gathers, scuppers are placed there to protect entrances and deckhouses from water
logging. Freeing ports are placed along open bulwarks to rapidly release large volumes of seawater from the
main deck, preventing pocketing that compromises stability. These are large openings in the bulwarks intended
to quickly remove massive quantities of water entered in to open areas during heavy weather, preventing the
accumulation of weight on deck. Both systems are critical for maintaining stability and preventing structural
damage.
The distinction is one of duty. A scupper is a small drain through the deck or bulwark, piped overboard,
sized to clear rain and spray continuously from a local low spot — which is why it belongs where the
superstructure creates a pocket. A freeing port is a large opening at deck level in the bulwark, sized by
rule against the length of the bulwark, and its duty is to clear a boarding sea in seconds — which is why it
belongs on the open run of weather deck where green water actually lands.
b) It is essential that scuppers and freeing ports are operational at all times to ensure;
1. Water Drainage: Scuppers allow water that accumulates on deck to drain overboard, preventing excessive
weight and potential instability.
2. Free surface effect, raising COG, and reducing freeboard: Freeing ports facilitate quick drainage of
water from enclosed decks. If these systems fail, water can pool on deck, increasing free surface effect and
raising COG. Accumulated water adds significant weight, reducing the vessel's freeboard.
3. Safety During Operations: During rough seas, operational scuppers help maintain a clear deck by
preventing water accumulation, which could create slippery surfaces and increase the risk of accidents among
crew members.
4. Compliance with Regulations: Keeping scuppers and freeing ports operational is essential by regulation
24 of International Convention on Load Lines (ILLC). Non-compliance can lead to penalties, and detention of the
vessel until issues are resolved. The two arrangements sit under different regulations and should be quoted
separately: scuppers, inlets and discharges are ILLC Regulation 22, freeing ports are ILLC
Regulation 24. Both are conditions of assignment of the freeboard, so a defective arrangement puts the
load line certificate in question and not merely the drainage.
c) Oil tankers have handrails on the main cargo deck, beyond personnel safety, for the following reasons,
i) Handrails ensure that any green seas are drained very quickly from the deck, this prevents an increase in
stress on the vessel that would be produced if the extra mass of water was retained on board.
ii) The use of guard rails makes a saving in construction costs, as less steel is used.
iii) Large volumes of water, if retained on deck, could possibly affect the vessels stability by raised COG, free
surface effect and reduced free board, and by fitting handrails this will ensure that water drains quickly.
The reasoning to spell out is that open rails, fitted instead of solid bulwarks, let a shipped sea clear
straight off the deck edge with nothing to hold it. A loaded tanker has very little freeboard and ships water
readily, so a solid bulwark on a tanker's cargo deck would trap large volumes of water between the rails and the

tank tops. Open rails therefore prevent water trapping, remove the added weight and free surface before they
can act, and remove the racking and sloshing loads that a trapped body of water would impose on the deck
and the bulwark itself. Note also that the rule allowing freeing-port area to be credited as a fraction of the
bulwark length does not arise where open rails are fitted, because there is no bulwark to pierce.
Source note: Part 2's original part (b)4 puts both scuppers and freeing ports under ILLC Regulation 24, and its own Model
Additions box records that these are different regulations — scuppers and discharges Regulation 22, freeing ports Regulation 24.
The original sentence is preserved above and the split is given immediately after it. The same slip appears in the March 2019
printing of the neighbouring question and is corrected the same way in E42.

E42.title: Watertight & weathertight doors — function and location; scuppers &
E42.answer_markdown:
Definitions first — the marks are in them
Watertight means the closure withstands a design head of water from either side without leakage, and
watertight closures are fitted below the bulkhead or freeboard deck. Weathertight means water will not
penetrate into the ship in any sea condition, and weathertight closures are fitted at openings in exposed
positions on and above the freeboard deck. The difference is a static head from either side versus no
penetration from outside in the intact condition.
(a) (i) Watertight doors: Watertight doors on ships are critical safety barriers designed to prevent the spread
of flooding between compartments during emergencies limiting the spread of water within the vessel and help
maintain its buoyancy and stability. They are essential in any opening that compromises the watertight integrity
of the ship's hull. These doors are installed below the waterline in areas prone to flooding such as: Shaft tunnels
· Ballast tanks · Engine room bulkheads · Pipe tunnels.
(ii) Weathertight Doors: Weathertight doors are designed to withstand weather conditions and prevent water
from entering the vessel during heavy seas or rain. They can withstand brief submersion. They do not provide a
fire rating: resisting the passage of fire and smoke is the duty of an A-class or B-class fire division, and a
weathertight door resists water from any direction in the intact condition and nothing else. Where a door has to
do both jobs it is rated twice over, as a weathertight closure and as a fire door. These doors are installed above
the waterline, in areas subjected to adverse weather conditions such as: Main Decks · Accommodation
Entrances · Navigation Bridge Entrances · Engine Room Entrance.
(b) It is essential that scuppers and freeing ports are operational at all times to ensure;
1. Water Drainage: Scuppers allow water that accumulates on deck to drain overboard, preventing excessive
weight and potential instability. Water logging can lead to corrosion, and structural damage.
2. Free surface effect, raising COG, and reducing freeboard: Freeing ports facilitate quick drainage of
water from enclosed decks. If these systems fail, water can pool on deck, increasing free surface effect and
raising COG. Accumulated water adds significant weight, reducing the vessel's freeboard. Taken together those
three effects are why trapped water is dangerous out of proportion to its weight: the added weight and the
raised centre of gravity reduce GM, the free surface of a body of water lying loose on deck reduces it again, and
the lost freeboard reduces the reserve buoyancy and the range of stability — so in a beam sea a deck-load of
trapped water can carry a ship past the point of return.
3. Safety During Operations: During rough seas or adverse weather conditions, operational scuppers help
maintain a clear deck by preventing water accumulation, which could create slippery surfaces and increase the
risk of accidents among crew members.
4. Compliance with Regulations: Keeping scuppers and freeing ports operational is essential by regulation
24 of International Convention on Load Lines (ILLC). Non-compliance can lead to penalties, and detention of the
vessel until issues are resolved. Quote the two separately — scuppers and discharges are ILLC
Regulation 22 and freeing ports are ILLC Regulation 24 — and add that both are conditions of
assignment of the freeboard, so keeping them clear and operable is a condition of the load line certificate
itself.

Source note: two corrections from Part 2's own Model Additions box are applied above. First, the original part (a)(ii) reads “They
can withstand brief submersion and provide fire and smoke containment, enhancing overall safety”; the box records that fire and
smoke containment is not a function of a weathertight door and instructs that the claim be removed, so that sentence is the one
place in this entry where original wording has been cut rather than added to — it now reads “They can withstand brief
submersion”, with the reason for the removal given in the text. Second, the original part (b)4 puts both scuppers and freeing
ports under Regulation 24; the sentence is preserved and the correct split, Regulation 22 and Regulation 24, follows it.

E18.title: Class A bulkheads & ventilation (accommodation)
E18.answer_markdown:
a) Class A bulkheads are structural divisions constructed of steel or equivalent material, suitably stiffened, and
designed to prevent the passage of smoke and flame for a designated time during a standard fire test.
Requirements for Class A Bulkheads are;
• Construction Material: Must be made of steel or equivalent non-combustible material securely stiffened to
maintain structural integrity.
• Fire Integrity: Capable of preventing the passage of smoke and flame for the designated time standard fire
test.
• Insulation (Thermal Performance): Must be insulated with non-combustible materials so that the average
temperature on the unexposed side does not rise more than 139 °C, and the temperature at any single point
(including joints) does not rise more than 180 °C within the following times:
◦ Class A-60: 60 minutes.
◦ Class A-30: 30 minutes.
◦ Class A-15: 15 minutes.
◦ Class A-0: 0 minutes.
One further line is a common discriminator between a pass and a strong answer. Integrity is judged against the
standard fire test (time–temperature) curve applied over 60 minutes. The suffix number — 60, 30, 15 or
0 — is the insulation period only, that is the time for which the temperature-rise criteria must be met; flame
and smoke must be held for the full 60 minutes regardless of the suffix. This is also the answer to the
March 2019 sitting's part (b) on the standard fire test for an A-60 division.

b) Design features of ventilation systems to prevent the spread of smoke and fire in Passenger Ship
accommodation are;
• Division by Main Vertical Zones (MVZs): Ventilation systems are typically separated according to the
ship's main vertical zoning. Ductwork serving one MVZ should not pass through another, or if it does, it must
have robust, fire-resistant insulation to prevent heat transfer and fire spread across zone boundaries.
• Fire Dampers and Automatic Closure: Ventilation trunkings must be able to maintain the fire integrity of
the bulkhead or deck through which it passes. Ducts passing through bulkhead divisions must have
automatic fire dampers with manual operation facility from both sides of the bulkhead with open-closed
indicator.
• Duct Material and Construction: Ducts passing through accommodation areas must be constructed of
steel or equivalent non-combustible materials to ensure they do not catch fire themselves.
• Isolation and Control: Atriums shall be within enclosures formed of Class A divisions. Atriums shall be
equipped with a smoke extraction system. The smoke extraction system shall be activated by the detection
system and be capable of manual control. The fans shall be sized such that the entire volume within the
space can be exhausted in 10 min or less.
• Smoke and Fire Containment: The ventilation system is designed to be easily controlled, allowing for the
immediate shutting down of fans in the event of a fire, reducing oxygen supply and preventing the smoke
from being circulated throughout accommodation.
• Location and isolation of the plant itself: Where the sitting narrows the question to air-conditioning
units, supply and exhaust fans, add that AC units and fan rooms are located within their own A-class
boundaries, that supply and exhaust systems are separated by main vertical zone so that no fan serves
two zones, and that fans are provided with remote stops grouped at a control station outside the
space served, so that ventilation can be shut down without entering the fire area.
A dedicated safety centre as per SOLAS Chapter II-2, Part C, Regulation 23 manage fire doors, dampers, and
detection systems to contain smoke and fire effectively.
c) Class A bulkhead integrity in passenger ship accommodation is maintained at ventilation trunkings
penetrations by using steel sleeves, welding trunks directly to bulkheads, insulating them to match the
bulkhead rating, or by using automatic fire dampers, ensuring the boundary prevents smoke and flame passage
for 60 minutes.
To maintain the integrity of the bulkhead with respect to ducts having cross-sectional area exceeding 0.02 M²
must be fitted with an insulated steel sleeve unless the duct is made of steel. Ducts with cross-sectional area
exceeding 0.075 M² must be fitted with automatic fire dampers with manual operation facility from both sides of
the bulkhead with open-closed indicator.
Source note: Part 1 writes “SOLAS Chapter II-II”; corrected above to SOLAS II-2. Note also the part-order discrepancy flagged
with the question wording — in the March 2024 sitting the two sources disagree over whether the 5-mark part is the penetration
integrity or the ventilation design, so both are answered in full above.

E43.title: Class A and Class B bulkheads defined; integrity at doors & ventilation
E43.answer_markdown:
(a)(i) Class A Bulkheads: Class A bulkheads are structural divisions that are designed to provide high fire
resistance. Constructed from steel or equivalent materials. Capable of preventing the passage of smoke and
flame for a minimum of one hour during a standard fire test at 927°C. Insulated with non-combustible materials
such that the average temperature on the unexposed side does not rise more than 140°C above the original
temperature, and no point exceeds 180°C during the specified time.
The standard fire test is not held at a single temperature: it follows the cellulosic (ISO 834) time–
temperature curve, which rises to roughly 841 °C at 30 minutes and about 945 °C at 60 minutes. Class A
divisions are then rated by the period for which the insulation criterion is held — A-60, A-30, A-15 and A-0 —
while integrity against the passage of flame and smoke is maintained for the full 60 minutes regardless of the
suffix. So an A-0 division is still a one-hour barrier to flame and smoke; what it does not do is hold the
temperature rise on the far side.
(ii) Class B Bulkheads: Class B bulkheads offer moderate fire resistance and are made from approved non-
combustible materials, although combustible veneers may be permitted under certain conditions. Designed to
prevent the passage of flame for at least 30 minutes during a standard fire test. The average temperature on
the unexposed side must not rise more than 140°C above the original temperature, and no single point can
exceed 225°C within the specified time. Class B divisions are rated B-15 and B-0 by the insulation period, with
integrity for the 30 minutes of the test. The three differences from Class A worth stating are: B divisions need
not be steel or equivalent, their integrity period is 30 minutes rather than 60, and their single-point limit is
225 °C rather than 180 °C.
(b)(i) Doors: If the bulkhead has to be penetrated by a door, it must be of the approved type. The door should
be of the same material or higher Class "A" standard. The door must be fitted according to the classification
requirement. The door should have closing mechanism and should have self-latching and hold back are allowed
with remote activation or fusible link. Stated precisely, the door rating must match the rating of the
division — an A-60 bulkhead requires an A-60 door — and the door is type-tested and approved as an
assembly with its frame, hinges and securing arrangements, since a door leaf on its own proves nothing.
The door must be self-closing against a 3.5° inclination and capable of remote release from a continuously
manned control station, and no door in an A-class division may carry a louvre or ventilation opening.
(ii) Ventilation trunking: Ventilation trunking that is passing through bulkhead must be provided with sleeves
and dampers of suitable material. The dampers should must be provided with open close indicator. In practice
the trunk passes through a steel sleeve welded into the division, of the same thickness as the division, with
the insulation carried across the penetration; and at an A-class boundary an automatic fire damper is fitted,
arranged to fail closed, operable both automatically and by hand from either side, and provided with a
position indicator showing open or shut. Where a duct passes through the boundary without a damper, it
must instead be of the required thickness for a stated length either side and have no openings within the space
it crosses.

Source note: Part 2's original definition of a Class A bulkhead gives the standard fire test as being carried out “at 927°C”, and
its own Model Additions box records that the test follows the ISO 834 cellulosic curve rather than being held at one temperature,
and that 927 °C is approximately the 30-minute point on that curve. The original sentence is preserved above exactly as printed
and the curve is given immediately after it. The original also uses 140 °C for the mean-temperature limit; SOLAS states 139 °C,
and E18 carries that figure — either is accepted, but the two entries are not identical and the difference is noted here rather
than harmonised silently.

E19.title: In-water survey of a very large carrier
E19.answer_markdown:
In-water survey — preparation, operation and procedure. An In Water Survey allows for inspection of a
vessel's underwater parts while afloat, replacing one of the two required 5-year dry-dockings for vessels less
than 15-year-old. It requires approved diving firms, clear water, good visibility, and a clean hull. Put more
precisely, the survey replaces one of the two bottom inspections required within a five-year special-
survey cycle; it is generally permitted for ships under 15 years of age, older ships being at the discretion of
the society; and the ship must carry the IWS class notation, with an approved high-resistance coating and
clearly marked draught and identification points on the hull.
Preparation: To facilitate the underwater survey, plans must be submitted showing the external features of the
hull below the sheer strake together with a key plan indicating the location of frames, bulkheads, weld lines, and
openings. Proper identification of hull markings is required to confirm location. The survey, including procedures
for viewing and reporting, must be approved in advance by the Classification Society.
Cleaning: The hull plating surface to be cleaned prior to the survey by Brush Kart. It is a hydraulically operated
vehicle with three brushing heads, it is drawn by a diver to clear the plating surface of all forms of marine
fouling.
Internal Inspection: Complementary internal examinations of tanks and spaces must be completed without
revealing significant damage.
Documentation: A Master's declaration of no damage, grounding, or unreported incidents must be submitted.
No CoC on hull and hull structure should be pending.

Vessel Condition: The ship should be at a light draft in sheltered waters. High-resistance hull paint is required
for the IWS notation.
Survey Vehicle (Scan): It is a self-propelled, steerable survey vehicle fitted with the following; A long-range
low light TV Camera to aid steering and check for hull distortion · A close view high-resolution color TV Camera,
to give a true picture of the state of the hull coating, and for inspections of weld seams · A 35 mm still Camera ·
An ultrasonic probe to measure plate thickness · A depth meter and a Speed indicator · An umbilical cable from
survey vehicle to survey Boat for electrical power supply to the hydraulic motor, and information transfer ·
Buoyancy spheres and compressed air bottle for floating of the vehicle.
Survey Boat: It houses the surveyor and consists of — A control console containing monitor, Plate thickness
printer, audio/video recording, and playback facility · Diver Communication System · Vehicle Control system and
associated instruments.
Survey Method: Certified divers use CCTV with two-way communication, allowing the surveyor to monitor,
direct, and record the survey in real-time; the surveyor must witness the survey in real time, not merely
review a recording afterwards. The survey vehicle is taken to the datum line by a diver. With the aid of TV
monitors and using the shell expansion plan as a map, the vehicle may be guided, from the control console,
over the bottom and sides of the hull by following weld-runs and other features such as inlets and tank plugs.
Pictures and information are relayed back and video recorded along with plate thicknesses giving the surveyor
an integrated visual record of all relevant information. Thickness gauging of suspect areas is mandatory.
Divers are also used for measurement of stern tube bearing wear down, rudder bearings/pintle clearances and
to inspect sea chests, valves, propeller, propeller shaft, stern seals, anodes, rudder, and rudder stock palm
coupling bolts — the rudder and stern-tube wear-down measurements being mandatory items. The
vehicle will also provide pictures of the stem frame, rudder, propeller, bilge, keels and hull openings.
Limits of the survey: The in-water survey cannot proceed if significant damage is suspected, or if there
are outstanding hull Conditions of Class; in either case the ship must be dry-docked.
Outcome: The diving company submits a final report containing all recordings and measurements. The
surveyor reviews the report, verifies all items are in order, and formally endorses the Class Certificate for the
“Intermediate Bottom Inspection,” provided all IWS requirements are met. If significant damage is found, the
surveyor may require the vessel to enter dry dock.

E20.title: Classification of ships & the notation +100A1
E20.answer_markdown:
a) IACS ensures ships are built to the highest standards, can operate effectively and safely, comply with strict
maritime and environmental regulations, and prolong their working life. Key reasons for building to classification
rules are;
• Safety and Integrity Standards: Class establish comprehensive rules for the design, construction, and
inspection of ships, ensuring they are structurally sound. These rules ensure the reliability of the hull,
machinery, and propulsion systems, effectively mitigating risks.
• Regulatory Compliance: Ships must comply with international conventions, such as SOLAS, MARPOL, Load
Line, Tonnage, and COLREGS which require adherence to the rules of a recognized classification society to
operate.
• Insurance and Finance: Classification is a prerequisite for insurance companies to classify a vessel as a
good risk, leading to lower insurance premiums. Banks also require this for financing, as it ensures the
vessel's asset value.
• Quality Control and Certification: The construction process is monitored by surveyors to verify that the
vessel is built in accordance with approved drawings and rules.
• Operational Requirements: A classification certificate proves that the ship is seaworthy, which is
necessary for charterers, bankers, and for operating in various ports.
b) According to Lloyd's Register (LR) classification society standards, the notation +100A1 represents the
highest-level classification for a seagoing ship. It is a steel ship built under special survey, suitable for
unrestricted worldwide service, with approved equipment. Meaning of the notation is as follows;
• + (Maltese Cross): Indicates that the ship is constructed under the special survey of the Classification
Society's surveyors, in compliance with their Rules and Regulations, to the satisfaction of the Committee.
• 100: Signifies that the vessel is considered suitable for sea-going service according to structural strength of
a steel ship designed for unrestricted navigation. Historically the figure is Lloyd's character figure, denoting
a ship built and eligible to be entered as first class (100A) in the Register for sea-going service.
• A: Confirms that the hull and its appendages have been built in accordance with the society's rules, and are
maintained in good and efficient condition.
• 1: Signifies that the anchoring and mooring equipment (cables, hawsers) are in good and efficient condition
and comply with the society's Rules.
For full marks, add that the notation is normally followed by a service or ship-type notation — for example
“Oil Tanker, ESP” — and sometimes by (E), indicating equipment to rule. Other societies use equivalent symbols
for the same meaning, for example DNV's ✘1A.
c) To remain in class throughout its life, a ship must adhere to;
• Surveys and Certification: Initial, annual, intermediate, periodic, renewal and special surveys on a five-
year cycle.
• Maintenance Compliance and Approval: Ensuring maintenance (PMS), repairs and upgrades are
approved by LR to maintain structural and mechanical integrity.

• No overdue surveys or Conditions of Class, prompt repair of any damage affecting class, and
compliance with the ISM and audit regime. Failing these, class may be suspended or withdrawn.
Note the weighting in this sitting — part (c) carries only one mark, so one line is enough and the time belongs in
part (a).

E21.title: Drydocking — pre-docking information & items to inspect once dry
E21.answer_markdown:
(a) Pre-docking information that should be provided to the drydock authority are:
• Vessel's Docking Plan: Docking plan is a technical drawing prepared during a ship's design phase that
details the underwater hull structure, including the keel, bilge keels, stabilizers, propellers, rudder, sea
chests, ICCP anodes, Speed Log transducer, Echo Sounder transducer, cathodic protection anodes and drain
plugs. It guides the shipyard on how to arrange blocks in a dry dock to securely support the vessel.
• General Arrangement Plan, Capacity Plan and Shell Expansion Plan: General Arrangement plan
provides a comprehensive overview of the ship's layout. Capacity Plan is used for calculating the vessel's
displacement and stability. Shell Expansion Plan shows the details of the hull plating.
• Stability Data: Provide the arrival stability condition, including Current Metacentric Height (GM), arrival
drafts (forward and aft), and trim, to ensure safe docking. Soundings of all tanks, ensuring tanks are either
completely full or empty to minimize free surface effects.
• Repair List: A comprehensive list of planned repairs and maintenance tasks that need to be performed
during the dry dock period.
• Tank Arrangement: Information on the tank arrangement and distribution, including any ballast, FW and
fuel tanks that may need to be adjusted before docking.

• The docking officer's landing data: the ship's weight and its longitudinal and vertical centres of
gravity for the landing calculation, and the declared trim on landing — a small trim by the stern being
preferred so that the stern lands first on the after blocks.
• Block and bilge-block plan: marked up to show every appendage, transducer, stabiliser fin, sea-chest
projection or sacrificial anode that the keel and bilge blocks must clear.
• Confirmation that the ICCP system is switched off and isolated before the ship enters the dock.
b) Once the dock is dry, the immediate inspection focuses on the hull, propulsion, and appendages for damage,
corrosion, and wear. Key items to be inspected immediately are;
• Hull Plating & Painting: Full inspection for corrosion, pitting, deformation, damage to paint coating, and
antifouling coating condition.
• Propeller and Rudder System: Checking propeller for damage to blades, fouling, and inspecting the rope
guard. Checking rudder for damage and checking rudder plug tightness.
• Sea Chests & Sea Valves: Inspect gratings and valves at sea inlets and sea chests to ensure they are clear
of obstructions and secured properly, together with the condition of the internal sea-chest anodes and
gratings.
• Anodes & Transducers: Inspecting sacrificial zinc anodes for wastage and ensuring ICCP anodes/
electrodes, Echo Sounder and Speed Log Transducers are in good condition.
• General Structure, Anchor & Cable: Inspection of the bow thruster tunnel, stern frame, anchor, bilge
keels, and any other appendages. Ensuring all tank plugs are secured and properly sealed, against a tank-
plug tally sheet recorded as plugs are removed and refitted.
Add the measurements that can only be taken with the ship dry, since these are what the docking is really for:
rudder pintle and stern-tube (tail-shaft) bearing wear-down by poker gauge, rudder and pintle
clearances, and propeller-cone and rope-guard security.

E22.title: Overhaul of ship-side valves in dry dock
E22.answer_markdown:
a) As Chief Engineer Officer, providing detailed information to the docking company is crucial for safe and
efficient valve overhaul. Essential information includes;
• Valve Identification & Location: A comprehensive valve list (location, type, valve ID, means of closure
(manual or power actuated), diameter, and flange PCD), with a marked-up plan showing sea chest positions,
including their precise location with frame number.
• Scope of Work: Clearly define scope of work including cleaning, inspection, packing replacement,
comprehensive overhaul, including valve seat grinding and testing.
• Material and Spares Availability: Clearly state which spares will be supplied by the ship (gaskets, nuts,
studs) and what is expected from the workshop.
• Isolation and Safety Measures: Hand over a clear procedure for isolation and safety measures prior
commencing the removal.
• Critical Timing: Clearly define the docking schedule, particularly the timeline for when valves must be
opened for overhaul and when they must be fitted back for re-floating.
• The survey requirement: state that these are classed items and that the Classification Society
surveyor must be given notice to attend, so that the yard plans the work around the surveyor's
availability rather than around its own convenience.
b) Key steps of overhauling procedure include;
• Dismantling: Ensuring proper isolation, remove the valve cover, gland packing, and spindle. Remove the
valve chest from the hull if necessary for extensive overhaul.
• Inspection & Cleaning: Clean all parts, remove rust/corrosion, and inspect for wastage. Check the valve
seating face for damage or pitting. Lap the valve seat and disc using grinding paste to ensure a proper seal,
lapping until a continuous contact band is achieved and proving it with an engineer's-blue check.
• Reassembly: Ensure all exposed steel parts are coated to prevent corrosion. Replace all worn-out studs,
nuts, and joints (graphite gaskets), renewing studs to the correct grade and tightening to the
specified torque. Apply anti-seize paste to threads.
• Function Test: Check the valve for smooth operation, opening, and closing properly. Conduct a hydrostatic
test to ensure the valve is leak-proof at testing pressure, and record the test pressures in the dry-dock
and class report. Ensure the overhaul is inspected and approved by a Classification Society surveyor.

Precautions to be taken before returning the ship to service;
• The survey and witness chain — the single most important precaution. Ship-side valves, that is sea
inlets and overboard discharges below the deepest waterline, are classed items. The Classification Society
surveyor should witness the opening up, the condition of the seat, the reassembly and the
hydrostatic test, all before the dock is flooded. Nothing should be closed up out of sight of the
surveyor.
• Positive isolation: confirm lock-off arrangements are in place while the valve is open, and that all blanks
and spectacle-plate isolations are removed before the system is returned to service.
• Securing the valve: Lock the valve in the open or closed position as required, ensuring the locking washer
and nut are secure. Verify that the valve operating handle is properly greased and the valve is functional
before flooding the dock.
• Final tally: account for every sea connection as closed and locked before flooding, against the valve
list handed over in part (a). This closes the loop and is the check that prevents a flooding incident on
undocking.

E23.title: Repair of defects on a solid propeller in dry dock
E23.answer_markdown:
a) Bent blades can be hot or cold straightened using a hydraulic press or mechanical tools designed for
alignment. The propeller is secured, and the bent section is carefully worked back into its original shape. Care
must be taken to avoid over-stressing the material, which could lead to cracks. In practice, straightening of
manganese bronze or nickel-aluminium bronze is done with local pre-heat rather than truly cold, precisely to
avoid cracking. After straightening, the blade should be inspected for any signs of fatigue or damage. After
repairs, the propeller must be balanced to ensure smooth operation.
b) Damaged blade tips can be repaired by metal arc welding or adding material to restore the original shape.
Using appropriate materials such as cast steel/copper alloys to weld a new tip onto the existing blade. Once the
new material is added, it is shaped and finished to match the profile of the other blades. After repairs, the
propeller must be balanced to ensure smooth operation. The repair should comply with IACS UR W24 guidelines
(welding especially below the 0.7 radius needs class approval), and post-repair non-destructive testing (NDT) is
necessary to verify structural integrity.
c) When pieces of a blade are missing, the repair involves evaluation of the extent of damage and determine if
the propeller can be salvaged or if it needs replacement. Blades are divided into three stress zones (A-highest,
C-lowest). Welding in Zone A (near root) is strictly controlled or prohibited. Pinning the zones to radius: Zone A
is the blade root and lower radii, roughly inboard of about 0.4–0.6 R on the driving face, where welding is
prohibited or requires special Class approval; Zone B is the intermediate region, where welding is
permitted by an approved procedure; and Zone C is the outer blade and tip, where repair is most freely
allowed. If salvageable, use metal arc welding techniques to build up the missing sections with compatible
materials. Either adding new metal to reconstruct the blade profile or casting a new piece to fit into the existing
structure may be necessary. The repaired area must be smoothed and finished appropriately, followed by
balancing the entire propeller to prevent vibrations during operation. The repair should comply with
classification society approval, and post-repair non-destructive testing (NDT) is necessary to verify structural
integrity.
Procedural controls applying to all three repairs. State these, because they are what examiners reward:
an approved welding procedure and a welder qualified for the specific bronze or alloy; controlled
pre-heat and interpass temperature; stress relief after any major build-up; dye-penetrant NDT —
note that the propeller is non-magnetic, so magnetic particle inspection is not used on it; and a final
static balance, with dynamic balancing for high-speed installations and controllable-pitch propellers.
Source note: Part 1 cites “IACS UR W24/W27”. Its Model Additions record that W24 is the propeller-repair rule and that W27
concerns stern-tube and shafting, so W24 alone is cited above.

E44.title: Dry dock specification — repair of ballast tank shell damage, and costing the repair
E44.answer_markdown:
Scope of Work: Removal and replacement of the damaged shell plating (approximately 2 m², 15 mm thick
steel), repair or replacement of damaged stiffeners, NDT inspection of adjacent areas for hidden damage, and
surface preparation (cleaning, blasting, painting) to the vessel's coating system.
Two items belong in the specification itself and are the ones most often left out. First, the material: state that
the new plate is to be of the same grade and thickness as the original and approved by class — 15 mm
to the specified steel grade — supplied with mill and material certificates, and that the repair itself is to be
to a class-approved plan. Second, the welding: require an approved welding procedure specification
(WPS) worked to by certified welders, with weld NDT by UT and MPI to a stated acceptance standard
and the reports submitted before the tank is accepted back.
Factors to Consider When Costing the Repairs: Material Costs (steel plates and stiffeners, procurement,
transport, certifications); Labor Costs (labour hours based on complexity, accessibility, shipyard rates);
Equipment and Tools; Additional Services (subcontracted NDT, surface prep, painting); Dry Docking Expenses;
Contingency budget for unforeseen circumstances.
To that list add the costs that a ballast-tank repair carries and a plate repair on open deck does not: staging
and access into the tank; gas-freeing and continuous mechanical ventilation throughout, because hot
work inside a wing ballast tank is simultaneously enclosed-space work and hot work and needs both permits, an
attendant and continuous atmosphere monitoring; the cost of the attending class and flag surveyor; and
the coating of the repaired area to the ballast-tank coating standard, which is a significant fraction of the job in
a narrow wing tank.
Repair Procedure: a) Preparation — schedule docking, allocate resources, obtain permits. b) Removal — cut
out damaged shell plating with clean, precise edges; remove damaged stiffeners; dispose of removed materials
per environmental regulations. c) Replacement — fit and weld new 15 mm plates with proper alignment and
welding procedures; install new stiffeners securely welded to shell. d) NDT Inspection — ultrasonic or
magnetic particle inspection of repaired and adjacent sections. e) Surface Preparation and Coating — clean
and blast, apply approved coating system. f) Quality Assurance and Control — strict adherence to standards,
regular inspections and testing.
Within that sequence, specify that the cut-out is taken to a rectangular insert with rounded corners, that
no new weld seam lands on or too close to an existing one, that the stiffeners are cut back and re-welded so
that the shell butt is welded first and the stiffener connections after, and that the welding sequence is
balanced to control distortion in a 15 mm plate. On completion the tank is hydrostatically tested to the
design head before the coating is accepted as final.
Documentation: Detailed repair report (work performed, materials used, QC measures), NDT inspection
reports, coating application records (type, thickness, method), and copies of relevant certifications, permits and
approvals.

E45.title: Aft end vibration on a new vessel — report to the Engineer Superintendent
E45.answer_markdown:
[The original answer is a formatted report to the Technical Superintendent. Its technical content is summarised
verbatim below; the letterhead placeholders are from the original.] Written as a report, it needs a heading, an
addressee, a statement of the observed symptom — severe vibration at the aft end at full service speed on a
new vessel — then causes, recommendations for this ship, and recommendations for the sisters still building.
Possible Causes for Aft End Vibration: a. Propeller Issues — the propeller could be imbalanced, damaged,
or experiencing cavitation. b. Shaft Misalignment — misalignment between the propulsion shaft and the stern
tube bearings could result in significant vibration. c. Structural Resonance — the design of the aft section
(stern frame, hull, supporting structures) may be prone to resonance and harmonic amplification. d. Machinery
Imbalance — imbalance or misalignment of engine, generator, or rotating equipment. e. Insufficient
Damping — inadequate vibration isolation systems or ineffective shock absorbers.
The cause to name explicitly, because on a new ship vibrating only at full service speed it is much the most
likely, is blade-rate (blade-passing) frequency resonance. The propeller exciting frequency is shaft rpm ×
number of blades, and its harmonics; when that frequency coincides with a natural frequency of the aft hull
structure or of the sterngear, the response is amplified and you get exactly the “resonance and harmonic
amplification” described above. The driving force is normally cavitation-induced pressure pulses on the
hull plating above the propeller — the propeller does not have to be defective at all, which is why the
vibration appears at one speed and not at others, and why it appears on a whole class of ships rather than on
one.
Recommendations: a) Propeller inspection and maintenance (balance, cavitation). b) Alignment check
between propulsion shaft and stern tube bearings. c) Structural analysis of the aft section to identify resonance;
reinforce or modify design. d) Machinery alignment and balancing. e) Enhanced vibration damping. f) Sea trial
and performance monitoring after implementing measures.
For this ship, order the work by what it will settle: take a vibration survey with accelerometers at the stern,
over a speed sweep, and identify the frequency and its relation to shaft rpm × blade number before anything is
altered — that single measurement distinguishes blade-rate excitation from an out-of-balance propeller or a
misaligned shaft. Then inspect the propeller for damage and blade-to-blade pitch error in dock, check the stern
tube bearing alignment and wear-down, and only then consider stiffening.
Recommendations for Sister Vessels Under Construction: a) Enhanced structural design with
comprehensive structural analysis and optimization to minimise resonance in the aft section. b) Quality control
during propeller installation (balancing, alignment, avoidance of cavitation). c) Standardized machinery
alignment and balancing procedures. d) Vibration monitoring systems for real-time tracking. e) Lessons-learned
documentation for future vessel construction projects.
Four specific measures should be named for the sisters, because they are what actually shifts the problem
rather than absorbing it:
• Increase the propeller tip clearance from the hull, so that the pressure pulse reaching the plating above
the propeller is reduced.

• Fit a highly-skewed propeller, which spreads blade loading over a range of angular positions and softens
the pressure pulse instead of delivering it as a single blow per blade.
• Change the number of blades, which moves the blade-rate frequency clear of the aft-hull natural
frequencies without changing the hull at all.
• Run a finite-element vibration analysis of the aft structure at the design stage, so that the natural
frequencies are known and kept away from blade rate and its harmonics before steel is cut.

E46.title: Standing orders — serious fire in the machinery spaces while in dry dock
E46.answer_markdown:
[The original answer is a set of standing orders under ten headings, reproduced in summary form:]
1. Immediate Response: Raise the alarm (activate nearest fire alarm, shout "FIRE!"); call for help (notify
bridge and dry dock management with location and extent). 2. Evacuation Procedures: Evacuate machinery
spaces and adjacent areas; proceed to the designated assembly point and report to supervisor. 3. Firefighting
Equipment: Use portable extinguishers (CO2 or foam) if trained and safe; do not take risks. 4. Isolation of
Equipment: Shut down machinery/electrical systems if safe; close fuel oil, lube oil and flammable liquid valves.
5. Communication Protocol: Maintain communication; report conditions and trapped personnel to emergency
services. 6. Fire Control Measures: Activate fixed firefighting systems (e.g. CO2 flooding) if applicable; assist
firefighters with vessel layout and hazards. 7. Post-Incident Actions: Account for personnel; do not re-enter
until declared safe. 8. Training and Drills.9. Reporting Procedures.10. Safety Equipment Checks.
The dry-dock specifics — where the marks actually are
A generic fire drill will not score this question, because the whole point of it is that the ship in dock is not the
ship at sea. The standing orders must therefore say, in terms:
• Who supplies fire-fighting water. The ship's sea suctions are out of the water and the fire main is
normally isolated and often opened up for survey, and the fixed CO₂ system may be isolated for hot work, so
primary fire cover is the shore or yard fire main and the dock fire party. The orders must state
where the shore connection is, that a charged shore-supplied hose is rigged in the machinery space before
any hot work starts, and who calls the yard brigade.
• Hot work control. No hot work without a hot-work permit, with the space gas-freed and tested,
combustibles removed or protected, a continuous fire watch during the work and for a stated period after
it, and boundary cooling and watch on the far side of any bulkhead or deck being worked on.
• The alarm must reach both ship and yard. Ship's alarms may be isolated during electrical work; the
orders must name the alternative means of raising both crews, since a fire found by a yard worker must
reach the duty engineer and a fire found by the crew must reach the dock.
• Escape routes and muster point change in dock. Access is by staging and a single brow rather than the
normal gangways, lifts and internal routes may be out of service, and there may be scaffolding in the escape
routes — so the orders must state the revised routes and the revised muster point, which is normally ashore
on the dock side, and must require a head count against both the crew list and the yard's contractor list.
• Before CO₂ is even considered, confirm that the space can be sealed and that nobody — including yard
workers who do not appear on the ship's muster — is inside it. Openings made for the docking work
commonly defeat the boundary, so the release decision in dock is the Chief Engineer's with the dock master,
not a routine action.

E47.title: Fatigue cracks in a ship's hull — why and where; the drydock hull inspection
E47.answer_markdown:
(a) Fatigue cracks in a ship's hull occur due to the repeated cyclic loading and unloading that the structure
experiences during its operational life. Ships are subjected to dynamic forces from waves, wind, and operational
maneuvers, leading to fluctuating stresses that can cause material fatigue over time. The inherent properties of
the materials used in the hull construction can contribute to fatigue. Poor design or inadequate structural
reinforcement in critical areas can lead to stress concentrations that promote fatigue cracking. Areas where
different materials are joined can experience high-stress concentrations, making them prone to fatigue cracks.
Structural corners or edges where changes in geometry occur often exhibit stress risers, leading to crack
initiation. The lower sections of the hull are frequently subjected to bending moments and shear forces from
wave action.
The mechanism to state plainly is that fatigue is driven by cyclic stress range acting at a stress
concentration — the number of load cycles and the local geometry, not weakness in the steel. A ship sees of
the order of 108 wave-load cycles in its life, and hull steel has no fatigue limit in a corrosive environment, so
cracking starts wherever the local stress range is raised by a discontinuity and is then accelerated by corrosion
pitting at that same point.
Locations where they may be found
The high-incidence sites, which is what the mark is for, are:
• Hatch-corner radii and the corners of deck openings — the classic site, because the deck is the most highly
stressed part of the hull girder and the opening interrupts it.
• Bracket toes, and the ends and heels of longitudinals, where longitudinal material stops or changes
section.
• Intersections of longitudinals with transverse webs, and the edges of lightening holes and cut-outs.
• Side-shell-frame end brackets on bulk carriers, top and bottom.
• Weld toes, and anywhere there is undercut or a poor weld profile.
• The sheer strake and bilge strake, and the ends of the bilge keel, where the keel is welded to the
ground bar.
(b) A comprehensive hull inspection during drydocking is essential for identifying maintenance needs and
repairs. Conduct a thorough visual examination of the entire hull surface for signs of corrosion, pitting,
deformation, and other anomalies, including checking for any visible cracks or weld defects. Inspect the
condition of protective coatings and paints; look for peeling, blistering, or wear that may expose the underlying
metal to corrosion. Use ultrasonic gauges to measure the thickness of the hull plates at various locations to
identify areas where corrosion has reduced material thickness below acceptable limits. Perform detailed
inspections of critical areas such as welded joints, brackets, and supports where structural integrity is crucial;
this may involve using borescopes to access hard-to-reach areas. Assess for any deformation in the hull
structure due to grounding or collision impacts, including checking for hogging or sagging along the length of
the ship. Open sea chests for cleaning and inspection of intake systems. Check sea valves for functionality and
signs of wear or corrosion. Record all findings systematically, noting locations, severity of defects, and
recommendations for repairs.
Name the methods and the framework, because “inspect for cracks” does not say how. Surface cracks are found
by magnetic particle inspection (MPI) or dye penetrant after the area has been cleaned to bare metal;
thickness loss and embedded defects by ultrasonic testing, taken to a set gauging pattern so that readings

can be compared with the previous docking and a wastage rate established rather than a single figure. The
whole exercise sits inside the class survey regime, and for tankers and bulk carriers specifically the
Enhanced Survey Programme (ESP), which requires close-up survey of nominated critical areas and
suspect areas, thickness measurement to a prescribed extent, and a thickness-measurement report
submitted to class. The hull condition monitoring and repair plan follows from that report.
Source note: Part 2's original part (a) offers “The inherent properties of the materials used in the hull construction can
contribute to fatigue” among the causes, and its own Model Additions box records that the driver is stress concentration
combined with cyclic stress range and not primarily material weakness. The original sentence is preserved above as printed, and
the corrected emphasis is given in the paragraph that follows it, so the mechanism written in the exam is the stress-range one.

E24.title: Survey & repair of a hollow rudder
E24.answer_markdown:
a) A thorough survey of a hollow rudder is essential for ensuring its structural integrity and functionality. The
following steps outline the procedure:
• Initial Inspection: Begin with a visual inspection of the rudder for any obvious signs of damage, such as
cracks or corrosion. This includes checking the alignment of the rudder with the stern frame and the
ship's centreline, and confirming that the rudder hangs true with no list of the blade.
• Water Entry Check: When the vessel is in dry dock, inspect for water ingress. Open the top and bottom
plugs to see if any water leaks out; if it does, this indicates a breach in the rudder.
• Pressure Testing: Conduct a pressure test with a water head of approximately 2.45 metres to assess the
rudder's watertightness. This helps identify any hidden leaks or weaknesses. Describe it correctly as an
internal head test: the rudder is filled through the upper plug to the specified head — often referenced to
the deepest waterline as required by class — and is then watched for a pressure drop, or for water issuing
from the lower plug, either of which indicates ingress. An air or vacuum test is the common alternative
where filling is impractical.
• Thickness Gauging: For older vessels or those with visible rust, perform thickness gauging on the rudder
plates to measure material loss due to corrosion.
• Clearance Measurements: Measure clearances between the pintle and bush in both longitudinal and
transverse directions. Standard clearances should be maintained to ensure proper function. Measure also the
jumping clearance at the pintle and the rudder carrier bearing wear-down.
• Condition of Anodes: Inspect sacrificial anodes for wear and replace them if necessary to prevent
corrosion.
• Percussion Testing: Use a hammer to perform percussion tests on the rudder to evaluate its condition by
listening for variations in sound, which can indicate areas of weakness or delamination.
• Stock and coupling checks: Examine the condition of the stock keyway, check the coupling-bolt
tightness at the rudder-stock palm, and carry out a freedom-of-movement check hard-over to hard-
over.
b) Depending on the findings from the survey, repairs may be necessary as follows:
• Corrosion Treatment: Areas affected by corrosion may require treatment or replacement of affected
sections of the rudder plate.
• Gouging and Re-welding: Cracks in welding seams or rudder plating are removed by grinding or gouging,
followed by re-welding using approved procedures.
• Bearing Replacement: If measurements indicate excessive wear in the bearings or if clearances exceed
allowable limits, replacing the bush or sleeve may be necessary.
• Straightening: Bent rudder stocks without fractures may be repaired by hot or cold straightening in an
approved workshop.
• Handling Twisted Stocks: If a rudder stock is twisted by less than 10 degrees, it may be reused (possibly
with a new keyway), but more severe twists require annealing or replacement.

• Controls on all repair work: all welding to a class-approved procedure with controlled pre-heat and
post-heat, NDT after repair, renewal of the anodes, and a re-pressure-test before undocking, with
the surveyor in attendance to witness it.
Source note: Part 1's first survey item reads “checking the alignment with the vessel's mast”. Its Model Additions record this as
wrong; the check is alignment with the stern frame and centreline, and that wording is used above. The head is also given as
2.46 m in Part 1 and 2.45 m in the Additions — either figure will be accepted, both being the same textbook value.

E25.title: Single vs twin propeller / rudder (wide-beam vessel)
E25.answer_markdown:
a) A single propeller and single rudder configuration are generally unsuitable for large cargo vessels with a wide
beam due to reduced maneuverability, increased risks of operational failures, and inefficient wake flow. The root
cause is the wake: a single screw on a full, wide, high-block hull sits in a very non-uniform wake field, which
drives vibration, cavitation and reduced open-water efficiency, and the rudder working directly behind it
is partly shadowed by the hull. Twin screws sit further outboard in cleaner flow. A further practical limit is that a
single screw of the power required may demand a diameter that exceeds the available draught and
immersion.
• Steering Challenges: For a very wide and large ship, a single rudder needs to be massive to produce
sufficient turning forces. This results in extremely high bending moments on the rudder stock and very high
hydraulic loads on the steering machinery, making the design impractical.
• Increased Drag / Lower Efficiency: Wider vessels face greater hydrodynamic resistance, limiting the
effectiveness of a large single propeller.
• High Risk of Cavitation: To achieve the necessary thrust on a wide-beam, heavy-displacement vessel, a
single propeller must be exceptionally large, which increases the risk of cavitation (vapor bubbles forming on
blades), leading to reduced thrust, noise, and structural erosion of the blade surface.
b) A twin propeller, twin rudder installation on large cargo vessels with a large cargo carrying capacity
significantly improves manoeuvrability, allowing for superior control in confined waterways, enhanced crabbing
abilities, and safer navigation. It offers high redundancy, where one propeller/rudder set can compensate for
failure, and enables better wake equalizing, reducing fuel consumption and vibration. The strongest points to
lead with are redundancy, manoeuvring capability and the shallow-draught benefit. Key advantages
include:
• Superior Manoeuvrability & Handling: The system provides better control at low speeds and improved
turning ability in restricted waters, often reducing the need for tug assistance during docking.
• Enhanced Reliability and Safety: Redundant systems ensure that if one propeller or rudder fails, the
vessel retains steering and propulsion capability.
• Increased Propulsive Efficiency: The twin arrangement improves wake equalizing, allowing for better
efficiency, reduced fuel consumption, and lower emissions.
• Superior Low-Speed Performance: It enables easier “crabbing” (moving sideways) by utilizing differential
engine thrust and rudder angles.
• Reduced Vibration and Noise: The improved flow of water to the propellers reduces vibrations throughout
the ship, improving onboard comfort.
• Reduced Drag: Twin rudder systems can allow for better propeller immersion and less cavitation.
• Reduced draught requirement: two smaller-diameter propellers can absorb the same power within a
restricted draught, which is the decisive advantage on a wide-beam, shallow-draught cargo vessel.
Although the question awards seven marks for advantages, a complete answer notes the trade-offs: higher
build and maintenance cost, additional appendage drag from the shaft brackets or bossings, and the fact
that a well-designed single screw is usually more efficient per kilowatt in deep water.

Source note: Part 1 lists “Improved Stability” — symmetrical thrust improving hydrostatic balance and reducing roll — among
the advantages. Its own Model Additions assess that claim as weak, since twin shafts provide little roll damping, so it has been
replaced above by the shallow-draught benefit. If you wish to include it, do so as a minor point and not as a headline.

E48.title: Large fixed bladed propellers — hull fouling, clean ballast running & the light propeller
E48.answer_markdown:
(a)(i) The effect of hull fouling: Hull fouling occurs when marine organisms such as barnacles and algae
accumulate on the hull and propeller. This increases drag and reduces the efficiency of the propeller. When a
propeller is fouled, it requires more power to achieve the same thrust, leading to decreased speed and
increased fuel consumption.
In propeller-law terms the fouled hull makes the propeller heavy running: the added resistance means the ship
makes less speed for the same revolutions, the wake is less favourable, and the propeller therefore absorbs
more torque at any given rpm. Its power-demand curve moves to the left on the power/rpm diagram,
towards the torque limit, so the engine reaches its torque or thermal limit before it reaches MCR revolutions —
the ship cannot make full power and full speed, exhaust temperatures and scavenge pressures rise, and the
engine is overloaded if the setting is not reduced.
(ii) Operation in clean hull, ballast condition: In a clean hull condition, the propeller operates efficiently
with minimal drag. The ship is typically in a balanced state, with ballast distributed evenly. The propeller
achieves optimal thrust with lower power requirements, enhancing speed and fuel efficiency. Clean and in
ballast is the lightest the propeller ever runs: the displacement and resistance are low, so for a given rpm the
propeller absorbs less torque and its demand curve lies to the right of the design curve. The engine can then
reach MCR rpm — and the overspeed limit — before it reaches full power, which is why the light-running
condition is limited by revolutions rather than by torque.

Engine power (% kW) vs % RPM — clean/ballast, fouled and light-running curves about MCR (original sketch, unaltered)
Part 2, p.49
Reading the diagram: the design or loaded service curve passes through MCR. The curve to the right of it,
reached with a clean hull in ballast, is the light-running line, and the curve to the left, reached with a fouled
hull, in heavy weather or when towing, is the heavy-running line. The vertical line at about 104 % rpm is the
speed limit and the curve above MCR is the torque and overload limit; the whole art of matching the propeller is
to keep the ship's operating point inside that envelope over the whole life of the docking cycle.
(b) A light propeller improves a ship's maneuverability, especially in challenging conditions, by increasing the
Light Running Margin (LRM) for better engine power during low-speed maneuvers. It also enhances fuel
economy by reducing drag and optimizing engine performance. Light propellers help vessels navigate "critical
speed ranges" more safely by increasing the power margin, reducing the risk of damaging vibrations. They are
designed to adapt to operational challenges like hull fouling and adverse weather, ensuring full power
availability when needed.
Put in engine-margin terms, which is what the question is really testing: a propeller is light when it absorbs less
torque for a given rpm, so its power-demand curve lies to the right — at higher rpm — of the design curve,
and the engine can reach MCR revolutions and full power before it meets the torque and overload limit. The
reserve between the running point and that limit is the Light Running Margin (LRM), normally specified at
about 4–7 % of revolutions, and it is built in on purpose at the design stage by matching a slightly under-pitched
propeller to the engine.
The reason it is built in deliberately is the whole answer to part (b). A ship does not stay new: as the hull and
propeller foul, and as the ship meets heavy weather or a head sea, the demand curve migrates left into heavy
running. If the ship had been matched exactly on the design curve when new, it would be over the torque limit
within months of leaving the yard. The LRM is the margin that lets the engine go on developing its full output, at
full revolutions, through the whole fouling-and-weather range without overloading — and it is why a new ship on
trials appears to be “over-revving” slightly for its power, which is correct and intended rather than a fault.

E49.title: Improving propulsion efficiency — ducted propeller (Kort nozzle) & Grim
E49.answer_markdown:
(a) Ducted Propeller (Kort Nozzle):
Ducted propeller / Kort nozzle (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.41
A ducted propeller, commonly known as a Kort nozzle, consists of a cylindrical duct surrounding the propeller.
This design helps to streamline the flow of water around the propeller, reducing turbulence and enhancing
efficiency. The duct accelerates the water flow through the propeller and reduces the effects of tip vortices.
Advantages: Increased Thrust (the duct concentrates the flow); Reduced Power Consumption; Improved
Maneuverability at low speeds. Disadvantages: Weight and Complexity; Cost; Potential for Cavitation if not
designed properly.
The mechanism is worth one more sentence, because it is what the marks are for: the duct is an aerofoil section
in its own right, and the acceleration of flow through it generates a forward force on the duct itself, so the total
thrust is the propeller thrust plus the duct thrust. Closing the tip gap also suppresses the tip vortices, which is
where a heavily-loaded open propeller loses much of its efficiency.
Be specific about when it helps. A Kort nozzle benefits heavily-loaded propellers working at low speed
and high thrust — tugs, trawlers, pusher craft and dynamically positioned vessels — and it can raise bollard
pull by a substantial margin. On a fast, lightly-loaded merchant ship the duct's own drag at speed
cancels the gain, and can leave the ship worse off than with an open propeller, which is why ducts are not

fitted to container ships. So the answer to “how is efficiency improved” has to be qualified by the loading
condition of the propeller, not given as a general improvement.
(b) Vane or Grim Wheel Aft of the Propeller:
Vane / Grim wheel aft of the propeller (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.42
A vane or Grim wheel is installed behind the propeller to harness the rotational energy left in the water after it
passes through the propeller. This device redirects the flow of water, recovering some of the energy that would
otherwise be lost as turbulence. Advantages: Energy Recovery; Reduced Wake Turbulence; Enhanced Thrust at
Low Speeds. Disadvantages: Increased Drag; Maintenance Requirements; Space Constraints.
The essential point about it is that the Grim vane wheel is free-running — it is not fixed to the shaft and is not
driven by the engine; it turns freely on its own bearing in the propeller slipstream, more slowly than the
propeller. It is also of larger diameter than the propeller, and that is the whole design idea, because the two
radii do two different jobs:
• the inner radius, inside the propeller race, acts as a turbine, driven round by the rotational (swirl)
component of the slipstream and extracting energy from it;
• the larger outer radius, outside the race in undisturbed water, acts as a propeller, using that extracted
energy to add thrust.
So the device recovers the rotational or swirl energy that a single propeller leaves behind in its race, which
is energy otherwise lost entirely, and converts it into useful thrust — gains of the order of a few per cent are
claimed. Its known weakness in service is blade fatigue and blade fracture: the outer blades are long, lightly
supported and pass repeatedly through the sharp velocity gradient at the edge of the propeller race, and
several installations have lost blades, which is why the device has not been widely adopted.
Source note: Part 2's original part (b) describes the vane wheel only as a device installed behind the propeller that redirects
flow and recovers energy, and its own Model Additions box records that this is not a correct description of a Grim wheel — the
essential characteristics being that it is free-running rather than fixed, and that its inner radius acts as a turbine while its larger

outer radius acts as a thrust-producing propeller. The original description is preserved above and the correct mechanism follows
it.

E50.title: Twin skeg rudders — why they are fitted & the advantages on high-capacity
E50.answer_markdown:
What a skeg is — define it before answering either part
A skeg is a structural extension of the hull that carries or encloses the propeller shaft and supports
the rudder — not an appendage bolted on, but shaped hull structure. A twin-skeg arrangement therefore puts
two shafts and two propellers under a wide, shallow, full-form hull, each in its own faired skeg with its
own rudder behind it. It is used on large bulk carriers, car carriers and LNG ships — beamy, high-block,
draught-limited ships — where a single screw would have to be either too large in diameter for the available
draught or too heavily loaded for the power being absorbed.
a) Reasons for Fitting Twin Skeg Rudders:Improved Maneuverability (two rudders allow more effective
directional control, especially at low speed such as docking or narrow channels); Increased Stability
(additional hydrodynamic resistance against rolling); Redundancy (if one rudder is damaged or inoperative, the
other can still function).
Lead, though, on the draught and loading argument, because that is the reason the arrangement exists:
splitting the power between two smaller-diameter propellers allows each to be fully immersed and lightly loaded
under a shallow draught, which a single propeller of the necessary diameter could not be. Redundancy is the
second real reason — a twin-skeg ship has two independent propulsion trains and two independent steering
gears, so a single failure does not immobilise her.
b) Advantages of a Twin Skeg Installation:Enhanced Propulsion Efficiency (improved flow of water
around the propellers, reducing turbulence and drag); Reduced Draft (shallower draft than traditional single
rudder systems, advantageous in shallow waters or depth-restricted ports); Improved Roll Damping (skegs
help dampen rolling motions); Better Course-Keeping (improved directional stability and control in rough
seas); Structural Integrity (distributes loads more evenly across the bottom structure); Less Vulnerability
to Damage (two rudders further apart, reduced risk of losing both to a single incident); Flexibility in Design
(naval architects can optimise the hull shape for performance while accommodating large cargo holds).
Of those, the three that carry the marks on a large-capacity vessel are:
• A better and far more uniform wake field. Each propeller works in the flow behind its own faired skeg
rather than in the thick, highly non-uniform wake behind a full-form single-screw stern, so propulsive
efficiency is higher and the cyclic variation in blade loading is much reduced — which means less cavitation
and markedly less hull vibration. On a beamy, blunt-sterned ship this is the dominant gain.
• The ability to fit two smaller-diameter propellers under a limited draught, each properly immersed
and at a sensible loading, so the ship can be built with the full block coefficient and cargo capacity wanted
without an unworkable propeller.
• True propulsion redundancy — two complete trains, which for a large gas carrier or car carrier is a
commercial as well as a safety argument.
Source note: Part 2's own Model Additions box flags “Increased stability against rolling” as a weak point — skegs add little roll
damping — and advises not leading with it. Both the part (a) item and the part (b) “Improved Roll Damping” item are preserved
above exactly as printed, because nothing in the original is removed; but they have been placed last in the order of merit and
the wake-field, draught and redundancy arguments put first, so that an answer written from this entry opens with the strong
material.

E51.title: Hollow rudder — the survey, and the effects of losing watertight integrity
E51.answer_markdown:
(a) A thorough survey of a hollow rudder is essential for ensuring its structural integrity and functionality. The
typical procedure:
• Initial Inspection: Visual inspection for cracks or corrosion, including checking the alignment with the
vessel's mast and overall appearance. The alignment actually checked is the alignment of the rudder stock
and pintle axis — that the stock, the neck bearing and the pintles are co-axial and that the rudder hangs
square in the stern frame — together with the jumping (lifting) clearance at the top of the rudder, which
is the gap that prevents the rudder lifting off its carrier.
• Water Entry Check: In dry dock, inspect for water ingress; open the top and bottom plugs to see if water
leaks out (indicating a breach).
• Pressure Testing: Pressure test with a water head of approximately 2.46 meters to assess watertightness.
• Thickness Gauging: For older vessels or those with visible rust, gauge the rudder plates to measure
material loss.
• Clearance Measurements: Measure clearances between pintle and bush in longitudinal and transverse
directions.
• Condition of Anodes: Inspect sacrificial anodes for wear and replace if necessary.
• Percussion Testing: Use a hammer to evaluate the rudder by listening for variations in sound indicating
weakness or delamination.
(b)[The original answer to (b) listed repairs — weld repairs, corrosion treatment, bearing replacement — rather
than the effects of lost integrity.] The effects of the rudder losing its watertight integrity are:
• The rudder floods and its submerged weight increases greatly. A hollow rudder is buoyant by design;
full of water it is not, and the whole of that added weight is carried by the rudder carrier, the neck
bearing and the pintles. Bearing loads and friction rise, the steering gear has to develop higher torque
to turn the rudder, and there is a real risk of overload of the steering gear or of the bearings seizing.
• Internal corrosion accelerates, and does so unseen. The inside of the rudder is not coated to the
standard of the outside and carries no anodes, so seawater trapped inside wastes the internal stiffening and
the plating from the inside, where no external inspection will find it. The plate can be sound on the outside
and wasted through on the inside.
• A free-surface and weight effect, where the flooded volume is large — a change of trim by the stern and,
with the rudder partly full, water surging inside it as the ship rolls and as the rudder is put over.
• Ice damage in freezing service. Water trapped inside the rudder that freezes expands and can split the
rudder plating from within, converting a small leak into a structural failure.
• The loss of the leak test as a monitoring tool. Once the rudder is known to be flooded, the annual drain-
plug check no longer tells you anything new, and the class implication is that the rudder must be opened up,
the source of ingress found and repaired, and the rudder re-tested to the design head before it is accepted.
Source note: two corrections from Part 2's own Model Additions box are applied above. First, part (b) as printed answers a
different question — it lists repairs rather than the effects of lost watertight integrity — and Part 2 records that and supplies the
effects; the bracketed record of what the original contained is preserved above and the effects are answered in full. Second, the
original part (a) checks “alignment with the vessel's mast”, which Part 2 identifies as an error: rudder alignment is checked
against the rudder-stock and pintle axis and the jumping clearance, not the mast. The original wording is preserved and the
correct check follows it.
