E26.title: Tank inspections, erosion in ballast tanks & enclosed-space entry
E26.answer_markdown:
a) Items that should be looked for in a tank inspection;
• Structural integrity (cracks, fractures and grooving)
• General corrosion, pitting, blistering and coating condition
• Condition of Cargo Equipment
• Sacrificial anodes condition
• Internal pipework and fittings condition
• Tank openings and manholes integrity
b) Erosion in ballast tanks would be found around;
• Underneath the Bell-Mouth: Severe pitting corrosion often occurs on the bottom plating directly below the
suction pipes (bell-mouth) due to high-velocity water movement and vortex action during stripping
operations. Strictly this is erosion-corrosion: the protective scale or coating is mechanically swept away by
the high-velocity flow, and the bare steel then corrodes.
• Bottom Plating & Suction Wells: Areas where sediment retention is high are prone to microbiologically
induced corrosion.
• Areas of coating breakdown, where the paint film has already failed and the exposed steel is subject to
flow.
• The waterline or part-full band — the zone that is alternately wet and dry as the tank is filled and
emptied. This is the worst corrosion zone in a ballast tank and is the location most candidates omit; naming it
earns the mark.

c) Enclosed Space Entry procedure according to COSWP 2025;
• Pre-Entry Planning: Conduct a risk assessment to identify potential hazards (oxygen depletion, toxic/
flammable gases, slip, trip, fall and entrapment) and implement control measures. Develop an entry plan
that outlines the tasks to be performed and safety measures.
• LOTO and Atmosphere Testing: Ventilate the space thoroughly. Isolate all connecting pipelines, machinery
and tag out (LOTO). Test the atmosphere using calibrated gas detectors at various levels (top, middle,
bottom). Keep ventilation running during entry and re-test periodically, particularly after breaks. Entry should
proceed only once the readings confirm oxygen at 20.9% by volume, and hydrocarbon and toxic gas — for
example hydrogen sulphide and carbon monoxide — within their permitted limits.
• Safety Equipment: Rescue equipment (tripod, stretcher, SCBA, first aid) must be ready at the entrance with
designated rescue party. Entrants must wear appropriate PPE, including personal gas monitor, harness,
lifeline, safety torch and EEBD (for emergency use).
• Enclosed Space Entry Permit and Tool Box meeting: Complete an Enclosed Space Entry Permit
confirming that the hazards of the job and of the space have been dealt with. Ensure all personnel involved
are aware of the task, the hazards, and are competent in their job. The permit must be time-limited and
re-validated after any break in the work, consistent with the requirement to re-test the atmosphere.
• Authorized Entry and Monitoring: A trained person/safety officer must be posted at the entrance to
establish clear communication protocols through radio and monitor the entry process. If any person feels
unwell, or if the oxygen level drops/gas alarm sounds, the space must be evacuated immediately. On
completion, the space is secured, and the permit is closed.

E27.title: Anchor cable attachment & chain locker
E27.answer_markdown:
a) A clear sketch of attaching the bitter end of anchor cable to ships structure is given below. The bitter end of
the anchor chain is released in an emergency by removing a safety pin and driving out a locking pin from the
securing bracket using a dedicated emergency sledge hammer (painted in red color).
The marking point in this part is that the cable must be releasable from a safe position. The bitter end is
secured by a weak-link bracket or slip — for example a senhouse slip, or a clenched ring retained by a
release pin — arranged so that it can be operated from outside the chain locker, normally from the deck or
the compartment above. State explicitly that the release arrangement must not require anyone to enter
the locker, because the chain locker is an enclosed space and entry in an emergency would be impossible.
That is the point the examiner is testing, and the sketch should show the release pin and its operating position
accordingly.
Original sketch — bitter-end attachment to bulkhead, plan view (preserved unaltered) Part 1, p.23
(b) Chain lockers are emptied of water and silt using a dedicated drainage eductor. The eductor uses a high-
velocity jet of sea water (motive water) from the fire main system, which creates a suction that draws out water,
mud, and silt from the chain locker sump. The effluent is generally mixed with the motive water before being
discharged overboard. As chain locker is pumped out, fire main water is sprayed into the locker to flush out any
remaining sediment or mud.

Restrictions that may have to be observed while discharging chain locker effluent are;
• Anchor chain must be carefully and thoroughly washed down as it is being hauled out of the water to remove
sediment and organisms.
• Rinsing or pumping out chain lockers is prohibited in port to avoid the adverse effects of non-native species
introduction.
• At least once per month, the rinsing or pumping out of chain lockers must occur as far from shore as possible
and, if technically feasible, the rinsing or pumping out of chain lockers must not occur in US federally-
protected waters / special areas.
c) Dangers associated with entering a chain locker as per Enclosed Space Entry guidelines of COSWP 2025 are;
• Oxygen Deficiency/Asphyxiation — arising chiefly because the rusting of the chain and of the locker
steel consumes the oxygen in the space, which is the cause worth naming.
• Accumulation of Toxic / Flammable Gases
• Inadequate Ventilation
• Slip, trip, fall and entrapment (especially if chains shift unexpectedly while working inside).
Entry therefore requires a full enclosed-space-entry permit, with atmosphere testing, forced ventilation and
a standby man posted at the access.

E53.title: Defects in the steelwork of ballast tanks — causes, areas affected &
E53.answer_markdown:
(a) Factors That May Cause Defects:Corrosion (general corrosion, pitting, and microbial influenced
corrosion (MIC), exacerbated by inadequate coating and contaminants); Poor Maintenance (failure to clean
tanks or inspect/replace gaskets and seals; poorly secured manhole covers allowing water ingress); Stress
Concentrations (at welds, fittings, or areas where temporary lifting devices were used during construction;
repeated loading/unloading cycles causing fatigue fractures); Operational Practices (improper ballasting/
deballasting introducing excessive forces; rapid filling or emptying creating pressure surges).
Underlying all of them is coating breakdown followed by alternate wetting and drying: a dedicated
seawater ballast tank spends its life half full or empty, so the steel is repeatedly wetted with aerated seawater
and then exposed to air, which is the most aggressive corrosion regime there is — plenty of oxygen and plenty
of electrolyte, in turn.
(b) Areas Most Likely to Be Affected:Tank Bottom (bottom plating particularly susceptible to erosion and
corrosion due to sediment accumulation and stagnant water; indicated by visible rust or pitting and by
ultrasonic thickness measurements revealing material loss); Weld Seams (common points for stress
concentration and potential failure; indicated by visible cracks or deformations, detected by visual inspection or
NDT such as dye penetrant or ultrasonic testing).
Four further zones should be named, with the reason in each case:
• The tank top and under-deck plating, where warm humid air condenses on the underside of a sun-heated
deck and drips back — corrosion from above, in a place nobody looks at from the bottom of the tank.
• The air–water interface, the “waterline band” — the band of plating and structure at the level the
ballast normally sits at. Alternating wet and dry with a plentiful oxygen supply gives the worst pitting
anywhere in the tank, and it is the classic finding of a ballast tank survey.
• Horizontal surfaces that hold water — flange faces, bracket toes, the tops of stiffeners and girder faces
— because water standing on a horizontal ledge never dries and the coating fails there first.
• Around heating coils, where the local temperature accelerates the reaction, and at the suction bell-
mouth, where high local velocity strips the coating and the corrosion product together — erosion-
corrosion.
(c) Methods to Minimise Damage:Regular Inspections and Maintenance (rigorous inspection schedule,
routine checks for corrosion and structural integrity, regular cleaning to remove sediment and contaminants);
Coating and Cathodic Protection (high-quality protective coatings to reduce corrosion rates; cathodic
protection systems such as sacrificial anodes to mitigate galvanic corrosion).
Name the standard and state how the two protections divide the work. Coatings for dedicated seawater ballast
tanks are applied to the IMO PSPC — the Performance Standard for Protective Coatings — which
specifies a coating system with a 15-year target useful life, together with the surface preparation, edge
treatment, film thickness and inspection needed to achieve it. Coatings and anodes are then complementary,
not alternatives: the coating is the primary barrier, and the anodes protect the bare steel at coating
holidays, damage and breakdown. The corollary is worth stating because it is often missed — anodes only
work where the steel is wet, so in a tank that is frequently empty the anodes give no protection at all for
much of the time and the coating is doing the whole job.

E28.title: Ballast Water Management Convention
E28.answer_markdown:
a) The International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships' Ballast Water and Sediments, 2004
aims to:
• Prevent the Spread of Invasive Species: The primary goal is to minimize the transfer of harmful aquatic
organisms and pathogens through ballast water, which can disrupt marine ecosystems and lead to significant
ecological and economic consequences.
• Protect Marine Environments: By regulating ballast water management practices, the convention seeks
to safeguard marine biodiversity and protect coastal environments from the adverse effects of non-native
species introduction.
b) Difference Between Ballast Water Standards D-1 and D-2
• D-1 Standard: This standard requires ships to perform ballast water exchange in open seas, at least 200
nautical miles away from land (50 NM for shorter voyages) and in waters at least 200 meters deep. The aim
is to dilute and reduce the number of organisms in the ballast water before it is discharged. The volumetric
exchange efficiency must be at least 95%, which by the flow-through method means pumping at least
three times the tank volume through the tank. The 50 NM figure is the fallback provision — as far from
land as practicable, but not less than 50 NM and in water not less than 200 m deep.
• D-2 Standard: Regulation D-2 of the BWM Convention mandates that ships treat ballast water to meet
following discharge limits for viable organisms and indicator microbes using approved ballast water
treatment systems;
◦ Organisms ≥ 50 µm: Less than 10 viable organisms per cubic metre (m³).

◦ Organisms 10 µm – 50 µm: Less than 10 viable organisms per mL.
◦ Toxicogenic Vibrio cholerae: Less than 1 CFU per 100 mL.
◦ Escherichia coli: Less than 250 CFU per 100 mL.
◦ Intestinal Enterococci: Less than 100 CFU per 100 mL.
State the currency point explicitly, as it is often the key mark: D-1 is being phased out. All ships must meet
the D-2 standard, normally by means of an approved ballast water management system, by the implementation
dates, with full D-2 compliance required from 8 September 2024.
c) Documentation required, with reasons, by ships in international traffic to manage their ballast water and
sediments are;
1. International Ballast Water Management Certificate (IBWMC): This certificate confirms that the ship
complies with the Ballast Water Management Convention requirements. It is issued by RO on behalf of the flag
state and specifies which standard (D-2) the ship adheres to.
2. Ballast Water Management Plan (BWMP): Each vessel must have a specific plan detailing procedures for
managing ballast water, including operational guidelines for crew members. This plan must be written in a
language understood by the crew and include instructions for handling sediments, reporting requirements, and
emergency procedures.
3. Ballast Water Record Book (BWRB): This record book documents all ballast water operations, including
when ballast water is taken on board, treated, and discharged. It must also record any unusual events or
deviations from normal procedures, ensuring transparency and accountability.
4. Type Approval Certificate for BWMS: If a ship is equipped with a Ballast Water Management System
(BWMS), it must have documentation proving that the system has been type-approved according to
international standards.
5. Ballast Water Reporting Form (BWRF): Some ports may require this form upon arrival to ensure
compliance with local regulations regarding ballast water management.
6. Additional Documents: Certificate of Calibration, Training records, Commissioning Test Report, and, in
cases of exemption, documentation detailing voyages between specified ports. Following the 2020
amendments to the Convention, a BWMS must have a commissioning test with validation sampling

E29.title: IMDG hazard classes & dangerous-goods documentation
E29.answer_markdown:
a) Hazard classes of Dangerous Goods as stated in the International Maritime Dangerous Goods (IMDG) code
are;
• Class 1: Explosives — divisions 1.1 to 1.6
• Class 2: Gases — 2.1 flammable, 2.2 non-flammable non-toxic, 2.3 toxic
• Class 3: Flammable Liquids
• Class 4: Flammable Solids — 4.1 flammable solids, 4.2 spontaneously combustible, 4.3 dangerous when wet
• Class 5: Oxidizing Substances and Organic Peroxides — 5.1 oxidisers, 5.2 organic peroxides
• Class 6: Toxic and Infectious Substances — 6.1 toxic, 6.2 infectious
• Class 7: Radioactive Materials
• Class 8: Corrosive Substances
• Class 9: Miscellaneous Dangerous Substances and Articles
Only five classes are asked for, at one mark each, so naming five with their divisions is sufficient; listing all nine
costs nothing but earns nothing extra.
b) The documentation that must accompany any hazardous shipment:
• Dangerous Goods Declaration (DGD): This is a signed declaration by the shipper confirming that the
cargo is properly packed, marked, labeled, and in proper condition for carriage according to IMDG
regulations. It acts as a legal document identifying the hazards, enabling the ship's crew to take appropriate
precautions.
• Container/Vehicle Packing Certificate: Required when hazardous goods are loaded into a Cargo Transport
Unit (CTU). It certifies that the unit was properly packed, secured, and cleaned, complying with safety
standards.
• Special List or Manifest: The ship must carry a special list or manifest detailing the dangerous goods, their
classification, and their precise location on board. This is required by SOLAS Chapter VII and MARPOL Annex
III, and a detailed stowage plan may be carried in its place.
• Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS/SDS): It provide detailed info on physical properties, health hazards,
and emergency procedures.
• Document of Compliance for the carriage of dangerous goods: the ship-side document, required by
SOLAS II-2 Regulation 19, certifying that the ship's construction and equipment are suitable for carrying
the classes of dangerous goods listed on it.
These documents, along with the UN number, Proper Shipping Name, Class & where appropriate, the Division &
Compatibility group, Description of the goods with Gross mass/volume, Transport emergency cards (TREM cards)
and emergency contact information to ensure safe handling, stowage, and regulatory compliance must be
handed over to the ship's master or authorized representative prior to loading.
Purpose of Documentation
• Safety & Emergency Response: Enables the vessel's crew, port authorities, and emergency responders to
identify the exact hazard and take appropriate action in case of spillage or accident.

• Stowage & Segregation: Ensures hazardous goods are stored in compliant locations on board, preventing
dangerous reactions with incompatible goods.
• Legal Compliance: Certifies that the shipment meets international regulations, allowing it to be transported
through different jurisdictions.

E30.title: Noise levels on ships
E30.answer_markdown:
a) The unit of sound measurement is decibel, expressed as dB(A). dB(A) (A-weighted decibels), is a unit of
sound measurement that adjusts readings to match the human ear's frequency response. It filters out very low
and high frequencies that people hear poorly, making it the standard unit for measuring noise.
b) Based on the Code of Safe Working Practices (COSWP 2025) for Merchant Seafarers, MLC 2006 and The IMO
Code on noise levels on board ships, the noise level above which personnel are required to wear ear protection
is 85 dB(A).
Quote the figures from the Code on Noise Levels On Board Ships, resolution MSC.337(91), which is
mandatory under SOLAS II-1 Regulation 3-12. At 85 dB(A) and above, hearing protection is mandatory and the
space must be marked with warning signs; between 80 and 85 dB(A) protectors must be made available and
information given to the crew; and the daily exposure limit is L = 85 dB(A). The Code's space limits are
Aeq(24)
manned machinery spaces not exceeding 110 dB(A) with protection worn, unmanned machinery
spaces not exceeding 115 dB(A), and cabins not exceeding 60 dB(A).
c) A ship's crew can be made aware of hazards from excessive noise through a combination of mandatory
regulatory compliance, safety training on PPE especially uses of earmuffs, clear warning signage, and routine
inspections. These methods ensure that personnel understand the risks of noise-induced hearing loss and other
health issues, such as increased fatigue and stress.
d) i) Noise levels can be reduced in the design of Diesel generators by;
• Engine/Fan Design: Use modern engines with lower noise profiles and optimized, low-noise fan blades for
cooling.
• Exhaust Silencers (Mufflers): Install high-performance exhaust silencers to reduce 75% of noise
generated by exhaust discharge.
• Vibration Isolation: Incorporate rubber or spring anti-vibration mounts under the engine and alternator to
stop structural-borne noise.
• Resilient or double-elastic mounting of the whole generating set on a common raft with a floating
floor, together with an acoustic enclosure or lagging around the unit. This is the single strongest design
measure and should be named first.
ii) Noise levels can be reduced in the design of Ventilation Fans and Trunkings by;
• Fan Selection and Vibration Isolation: Use high-efficiency low noise fans with aerodynamic blades to
reduce source noise and install fans on anti-vibration mounts or pads to stop structure-borne noise.
• Flexible Connectors and Acoustic Duct Linings: Use flexible duct connectors between the fan and rigid
trunking to prevent vibration transmission. Lining ventilation ducts with acoustic materials can absorb sound
energy and reduce noise transmission through the ducting system.
• Splitter or attenuator silencers fitted in the trunking, and reduced air velocity in the ducts achieved by
generous duct sizing, since noise generated at bends and grilles rises steeply with velocity.

Half the marks are in part (d), and the question asks how noise is reduced in the design — PPE and operational
measures score nothing there.

E54.title: Harmonised System of Survey & Certification; the load line certificate
E54.answer_markdown:
a) HSSC: An IMO initiative to streamline and standardize survey and certification processes for ships. Main
objectives: Efficiency (harmonizing requirements across conventions to reduce redundancy); Consistency (a
consistent framework so vessels are assessed uniformly regardless of flag state); Simplification (clear guidelines
reducing confusion and administrative burden); Interoperability (better cooperation between classification
societies and regulatory bodies, mutual recognition of surveys and certificates).
The defining mechanism has to be given, because the objectives on their own do not explain what the system
actually does. HSSC sets a five-year certificate cycle for all the convention certificates, with annual,
intermediate and renewal surveys aligned so that the SOLAS, MARPOL, Load Line, IOPP, Tonnage and other
surveys fall together rather than at scattered dates through the year. Each is tied to a single anniversary
date, and each survey may be carried out within a survey window of ±3 months about that anniversary
date. That is the point of the whole scheme: one attendance instead of several, no certificate quietly expiring
between dockings, and a window wide enough that surveys can be planned around the ship's trading pattern.
b) Inspection Items Related to Load Line Certificate:Hull Condition (corrosion, damage, structural
integrity affecting buoyancy and stability); Load Line Marks (correctly displayed, visible, accurately reflecting
assigned freeboard); Hatch Covers and Closing Appliances (watertight and in good working condition);
Freeing Ports and Scuppers (unobstructed and functioning); Stability Information (up-to-date
documentation); Maintenance Records (regular inspections conducted).
Keeping Items in Compliance: Regular Surveys (annually or every five years); Maintenance Protocols for all
load-line fittings; Documentation Updates; Training and Awareness of crew. Stated against the HSSC cycle, that
means a Load Line renewal survey every five years, with an annual survey in each intervening year,
each within the ±3-month window.
The link that must be made explicit is that the items listed are not an arbitrary inspection list — they are
precisely the conditions of assignment of the freeboard. The freeboard was assigned on the assumption that
the closing appliances are weathertight, that the freeing ports and scuppers will clear water from the deck, that
the guard rails and means of access protect the crew, and that the marks are correct and visible. Keeping those
items in order is therefore what keeps the assigned freeboard valid, and a defect in any of them is a defect in
the certificate itself and not merely a maintenance item.

E55.title: Five methods of preventing distortion of plates and frames during welded
E55.answer_markdown:
FIVE methods to prevent distortion: (1) weld both sides; (2) back-step welding; (3) skip / wandering technique; (4) toggle-plate
welding; (5) sequence welding (original sketch, unaltered) Part 2, p.43
FIVE methods to prevent distortion: (1) weld both sides; (2) back-step welding; (3) skip / wandering technique;
(4) toggle-plate welding; (5) sequence welding. Because this is a 10-mark sketch question, the sketches alone
will not carry it — each one must be annotated with the principle that makes it work, and that annotation is
what earns the marks:
1. Weld both sides — balanced or double-sided welding. Depositing equal weld metal either side of
the plate equalises the shrinkage about the neutral axis, so the angular contraction of one side is
cancelled by the other and the plate stays flat instead of pulling into a vee.
2. Back-step welding. Short runs are deposited in the reverse direction to the general direction of
travel, so that each run's contraction opposes the last and the accumulated longitudinal shrinkage is
broken up into short, self-cancelling lengths instead of building up along the seam.
3. Skip or wandering technique. Runs are deposited in a scattered order along the joint rather than
consecutively, which spreads the heat input and avoids a local build-up of temperature — it is
uneven heating that distorts, so distributing the heat distributes the strain.

4. Toggle-plate welding — tack and strongback restraint. Toggle plates, strongbacks or tack-welded
bridging pieces hold the plates mechanically to the set gap and in plane while the weld cools, so
the joint cannot close up or lift; they are removed and the marks dressed off afterwards.
5. Sequence welding — a balanced welding sequence. The sequence is planned to work outward
from the centre of the panel or the repair, so that shrinkage is drawn toward the middle and the free
edges are left free to move rather than being restrained into locked-in stress.
Two further recognised methods are worth adding if more than five are wanted, or as supporting comment: pre-
setting and pre-cambering, in which the plates are deliberately set out of line by the amount the weld is
expected to pull them, so that the shrinkage brings the work to the correct shape; and controlled heat input
— low-hydrogen consumables, the correct run size and a limited interpass temperature — since the total heat
put into the joint is the ultimate driver of how much it will move.

E56.title: Propeller slip — definition, calculation & the conditions that affect it
E56.answer_markdown:
a) Propeller Slip is the difference between the theoretical distance a propeller should travel in one complete
revolution (based on its pitch) and the actual distance it travels through the water. Slip % = (Theoretical Speed
− Actual Speed) / Theoretical Speed × 100, where Theoretical Speed is calculated from the propeller's pitch and
the engine's RPM, and Actual Speed is the speed of the vessel through the water.
There are two slips, and the definition should distinguish them, because they answer different questions:
• Apparent slip = (engine speed − ship's speed) / engine speed, where engine speed = pitch × rpm and
the ship's speed comes from the log. It is the figure worked out in the engine room from the counter and
the log, and it is the one normally meant by “slip” on a daily report.
• Real slip = (engine speed − speed of advance V ) / engine speed, where V = V(1 − w) and w is the wake
a a
fraction. It uses the speed of the water actually arriving at the propeller disc, which is less than the ship's
speed because the propeller works inside the hull's own wake.
The consequence follows from the definitions: real slip is always positive, because the propeller must always
advance less than its pitch to generate thrust, whereas apparent slip can go negative — with a following
current or a following sea, the ship is being carried along faster than the propeller is driving her, and the
arithmetic returns a negative figure. A negative apparent slip is therefore not an error and not an impossibility;
it is information about the current.
b) Conditions Affecting Propeller Slip:Hull Condition (a fouled or damaged hull increases drag, leading to
higher slip); Speed of the Vessel (as speed increases, slip typically decreases); Propeller Design (diameter,
pitch, and blade shape impact efficiency — larger diameter propellers generally have less slip); Environmental
Conditions (wind, current, and sea state — operating against a strong current or in heavy seas increases
resistance and slip).
For a displacement merchant ship the four conditions to give, with the reason in each case, are:
• Hull and propeller fouling. Added resistance means the ship makes less speed for the same revolutions,
so slip rises — which is exactly why slip is logged daily: a steadily rising slip on unchanged draught and
weather is the standard indicator of a fouled hull and the trigger for a hull clean.
• Head seas and heavy weather. Added resistance and the loss of speed in a head sea raise slip; a following
sea lowers it, and can drive apparent slip negative.
• Shallow water. The restricted flow under the hull increases resistance and changes the wake field — the
shallow-water effect — and slip rises noticeably before any change in draught or weather.
• Increased draught and displacement. A deeper ship has more resistance for the same revolutions, so a
loaded passage shows a higher slip than the same ship in ballast.
The wake fraction is the underlying reason apparent and real slip differ at all, and it is itself a function of hull
form, draught and fouling — which is why slip is a useful performance indicator rather than a fixed number.
Source note: Part 2's Model Additions box for this question carries a correction reading that the “displacement vs planing
mode” reasoning applies to fast planing craft and not to displacement merchant ships. No such reasoning appears anywhere in
the original answer as Part 2 prints it, so the correction has nothing to attach to — like the welding-process correction recorded at
E37, it appears to be a residue from an earlier draft of the answer. The discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved silently, and
the substantive material that accompanies it — the four conditions that raise slip on a displacement ship, and the wake fraction
as the reason the two slips differ — has been written into part (b) above. Nothing has been removed from the original.

E57.title: TBT antifouling — why it was banned, alternatives, and selecting an
E57.answer_markdown:
a) The IMO has banned TBT antifouling coatings due to their detrimental effects on non-target marine
organisms. TBT is highly toxic and causes severe ecological damage, including hormone disruption in marine
species, leading to reproductive issues and population declines, and accumulates in the food chain.
Name the instrument and the signature damage. The ban is imposed by the IMO AFS Convention — the
International Convention on the Control of Harmful Anti-fouling Systems on Ships, 2001, which
entered into force in 2008 — and the specific effect that made the case against TBT is imposex in molluscs,
the development of male characteristics in females that sterilises the population, documented in the dog
whelk, together with shell malformation in oysters. TBT leached from hulls at concentrations of a few
nanograms per litre was enough to do it, which is why a coating on a ship became an international convention.
b) Alternatives:Copper-Based Coatings (base element: Copper — releases copper ions toxic to fouling
organisms, less harmful than TBT); Biocide-Free Coatings (base element: non-toxic polymers or silicone —
create a slick, low-adhesion surface that prevents attachment without leaching toxic chemicals).
Stated in the terms the industry uses, the two families are copper self-polishing copolymer (SPC), in which
the copper oxide biocide, usually with a co-biocide, is released at a controlled rate as the binder hydrolyses and
polishes away; and foul-release silicone or fluoropolymer coatings, which are biocide-free and work by
low surface energy — fouling cannot key to the surface, and what does settle is released by the water flow
once the ship is under way.
c) Considerations in Selection:Environmental Impact (minimal harmful leaching, compliance with IMO
regulations); Fouling Resistance (long-lasting protection against barnacles, algae, mussels); Durability and
Lifespan (withstand abrasion and impacts; longer lifespan reduces reapplication); Application Process (ease
of application, curing time, surface preparation); Compatibility with Existing Systems; Cost-Effectiveness;
Regulatory Compliance.
Two further drivers decide the choice in practice and should be given:
• Self-polishing versus hard or ablative behaviour. An SPC keeps a smooth surface and a predictable
leaching rate over the docking interval; a hard coating survives abrasion and ice better but loses its release
rate; an ablative wears away mechanically. The docking interval wanted — 30, 60 or 90 months — largely
dictates which is specified.
• The ship's speed and activity profile. A foul-release silicone needs water flow to shed settled fouling, so
it suits a fast ship on regular service and suits a slow or frequently idle ship very badly — and an idle ship
fouls fastest of all, since fouling settles in still water. The trading pattern, the proportion of time at anchor
and the water temperature of the trading area are therefore as much part of the selection as the coating's
own properties.
